speechtext: That the first report of the standing committee on estimates, presented to the house on Thursday, February 12, 1959 be now concurred in.

Mr. Speaker, once again we in this group would like to state our position in regard to this motion, and of course in regard to all similar motions. We have stated our case on other occasions, but I believe it serves a good purpose to take this occasion to state it again.
I realize that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) gave us an assurance the other day in this respect, and I wish to place on record at this point some of his remarks as they appear in Hansard. These are appropriate, I believe, and relate to the motion I intend to move. As found on page 989 of Hansard he is reported to have said:
-and I shall make it very clear that whenever the hon. members of this house fairly and responsibly find themselves in a position in which an injustice is being done in any way and the matter is brought to my attention, I shall do everything I can to rectify it.
Again, on the following page he went on to say:
I for one will say unequivocally that if at any time there is any action taken that would deny members of the opposition a fair opportunity of discharging their responsibility, I shall immediately see to it that a change is made in order to assure justice and fairness.
These words are very reassuring, Mr. Speaker, but I do not believe that is the way it was intended that parliament should be run. It is fine to have the assurance of the Prime Minister. He has certainly demonstrated in the past that he is very capable. He has certainly demonstrated that he has the loyalty and devotion of the members of the government. But there is one thing that we must always keep in mind, Mr. Speaker, and that is that individual members may come and go but governments keep on going. I am reminded of the immortal words of the poet Gray in his "Elegy in a Country Churchyard":
The boast of heraldry, the pomp of pow'r.
And all that beauty, all that wealth e'er gave,
Await alike the inevitable hour:
The paths of glory lead but to the grave.
In a recent television interview, Mr. Speaker, conducted by Mr. Pierre Berton, a personality in this country said that in his opinion the Prime Minister suffered from an enormous ego, and certainly the remarks contained in Hansard for last Friday bear out this point. I say it is far better that parliament itself should decide these things rather than any one individual, however capable he may be or however much loyalty he may command.
Certain rules have been laid down for the conduct of the business of this house. There must be a reason for them, and I think it is regrettable that it is becoming so habitual for these rules to be amended automatically at the first opportunity that arises in the house. I believe the rules of this house should be observed. Whenever the occasion and the need arise I am sure parliament will grant permission for these committees to sit while the house is sitting. I do not think this right should be granted automatically before the occasion has arisen.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch):
That the motion be amended by deleting the words "now concurred in", and substituting therefor the following:
"Referred back to the said committee with instruction to amend the same by deleting therefrom paragraph 3 which reads as follows: That it be authorized to sit while the house is sitting."

desire to say a few words on this motion. In so doing I want to make it very clear to you, although I know it is not required, that when I speak on a principle in this house it is the same principle upon which I speak or take a stand when in committee. I was at the organization meeting of the standing committee on estimates. In that committee I expressed my objection in a very few words, and I voted against the inclusion of this recommendation in the committee's report.
The main reason I rise is not only to express my objection to this procedure of a committee meeting at the same time as the house, but also because of something which I feel should be drawn very specifically to your attention as Speaker of this house and therefore guardian of the rights of all members of this house. I presume, sir, that applies not only to the House of Commons but to the committees of the house. I am going to say directly that in my opinion there has been and there is a conspiracy- legal, yes-so far as the relationship of government members and opposition members is concerned in the committees of this house.

There have been occasions in the past when a standing committee, at its first meeting, has recommended that the standing order be suspended and the committee allowed to sit while the house is meeting. There may have been occasions when, at its first meeting, a committee has recommended that the quorum be reduced from that established by the standing orders. But, Mr. Speaker, I am certain that while you have had the honour of occupying the high position you now hold, that has not been customary.
But, sir, what has occurred? At every meeting of a standing committee for organizational purposes during this session, two typed and prepared motions have been presented. One has been to the effect that the rules be suspended in order that the committee may meet while the house is sitting, and the other has been for a reduction in the quorum established under standing orders. As the committee work proceeds it is eventually found necessary to reduce the quorum or, to stick to the words of the motion, to sit while the house is sitting. This should be done, sir, as it is found necessary.
I think you, Mr. Speaker, being so intelligent, will understand that something must have gone on. As a matter of fact, I understand unofficially that some of the chairmen did not know about these motions being prepared until they saw them in front of them on their agenda when the committees met. With all due respect to the magnificent men who are the clerks of our committees, may I say that it is not their responsibility to draft agenda or motions. Therefore there seems to have been some direction. Then there is the fact that every committee has done exactly the same thing, something which was never done before. I say that this looks like a conspiracy against the opposition. Mr. Speaker, it is not possible for members of the opposition to carry on right from the beginning with a gun at their heads, and I say "with a gun at their heads" advisedly.
Oh, oh.

You have not the right to sit on committees, Mr. Speaker, but I can tell you this. That huge majority which the government has operates in committees in the same way it operates on the floor of the House of Commons. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is, for all committees at the same time, at the first meeting, a most unusual procedure. On the basis on precedents and on the basis of the true meaning of democratic parliament, as a member of this house speaking now as I voted in committee-thereby differing a little, may I say, from members of the official opposition who

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF COUNCIL TO ENCOURAGE AMATEUR SPORTS
PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF COUNCIL TO ENCOURAGE AMATEUR SPORTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give early consideration to the advisability of establishing a Canada sports council with the object of fostering and encouraging amateur sport in Canada, such council to have representatives from each of the provinces of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this most important public matter. It was just a little over two years ago that the prime minister of the day rose in his place and gave, in a most refreshing manner, the reasons why it was necessary to establish the Canada council. The Canada council was established, as you will recall, to assist the arts, humanities and social sciences.
The reasons advanced by him then for the establishment of the Canada council are
1038	HOUSE OF
Sports-Proposed Establishment of Council the same reasons that can be advanced for the establishment of a Canada sports council. If there was a need for a Canada council, then I submit that there is an even greater need for the establishment of a Canada sports council, because we are dealing with the health and fitness of the people of the nation. I do not know who said it, but it is true that a nation's health is a nation's wealth and we should not forget it.
In reading Hansard for January, 1957 I noticed that practically all members on both sides of the house strongly supported the establishment of the Canada council. The then prime minister also pointed out that practically all thoughtful Canadians who are really concerned about the future welfare of Canada also strongly supported the council. In reading the debates of that day I noticed also, Mr. Speaker, that the present Prime Minister spoke in favour of the formation of the council. He went on to say:
Indeed, the question has been asked on numerous occasions since 1951, why has the government delayed so long in the setting up of this council?
I do hope that all hon. members and the Prime Minister will have the same feeling toward the establishment of this sports council. I am sure that the early establishment of a Canada sports council would be welcomed in all parts of the country. I am sure also that under the inspiring leadership of the Prime Minister, early and sympathetic consideration will be given to this important matter.
In glancing at the first annual report of the Canada council one would seem to find confirmation of the views and opinions of those who advocated the council. I notice on page 20 of the first annual report of the Canada council the following:
In not a few places it has been gratifying to hear those responsible for local organizations say that in consequence of the council's help and recognition, local financial support has been increased and attendance enlarged.
The report goes on to say that during the 1957-58 season the council supported seven symphony orchestras. While the number of regular concerts given was the same as in the previous year, the number of performances for children and others was almost doubled, increasing from 93 to 175, and the total attendance increased from about 320,000 to an estimated 477,000. I am sure that if hon. members will support the establishment of a Canada sports council, the first annual report of the proposed new organization will be equally glowing.
I do suggest that if the sports council is formed the one paramount rule should be that the organization be as free from state


control as it is prudent for any body to be that is entrusted with public funds. I would further suggest that the general rules which now apply to the Canada council also apply to the proposed Canada sports council, with of course minor changes. I do suggest also, Mr. Speaker, that representatives from each province of Canada be appointed so that the organization will be a truly representative one.
The persons chosen, I submit, should be familiar with the great problems now facing all athletic clubs and all athletic associations from one end of the country to the other. The persons chosen should be prepared, I submit, to devote much time to the youth of Canada who desire to play games in national and international competition.
Now, Mr. Speaker, no one could go wrong in considering such men as Mr. Bob Osborne of Vancouver or the former mayor of Vancouver, Mr. Fred Hume. Then in Alberta there is one man who stands out, namely Mr. Mervin Dutton, who could add a great deal to such a council. The prairie provinces and Ontario could certainly contribute many worth-while people to serve. We could also well consider Mr. Melville Rogers of Ottawa, who has long been associated with the problems and issues facing athletic organizations in Canada. Then when you consider Quebec there are names that stand out as possibilities. I would suggest men like Cooper Smeaton, who has long been associated with the amateur athletic union of Canada. One of the members of the Molson family might also be a possibility, and there are men like Mr. Andy O'Brien, who has probably travelled with more Canadian teams than any other person in the country.
I do say, Mr. Speaker, that if help is given no one need fear any longer that Canada will rank behind England, Australia and South Africa. I feel that if help is given, at the next British Empire games Canada could possibly pull ahead of South Africa. If help is given possibly this country could once again see a truly national junior hockey final. The same remarks would apply to lacrosse. If help were given, I feel sure that we could do better in Davis cup play. We could do so much to encourage people to play badminton and so many of the other amateur sports.
One might ask, Mr. Speaker, how amateur sport is doing in Canada without adequate federal assistance. In summary, I would say that Canada is faring very poorly. For example, just last summer at Cardiff Arms park in Cardiff, Wales 33,000 spectators watched the closing events of the British Empire games. There were 250 reporters in the press box covering the activities of some

1,500 athletes from 35 countries. I submit that Canada put on a drab display. Canada's one gold medal came in rowing. In the final point standings we ranked fourth, well behind South Africa and a mere 100 points in front of Pakistan and the host country, Wales.
At the last Olympic games held at Melbourne in 1956, Canada gained only 52 points to place 16th amongst 44 nations. Hon. members will recall that last year in Davis cup tennis we played against a United States team that was virtually untested, and the United States team made a clean sweep of the five game series.
After the 1948 Olympic games, in fact after the 1952 and 1956 Olympic games, considerable publicity was devoted to what was called Canada's inadequate showing. I say to all hon. members that when thousands of people gather in stadia in so many different countries to witness our athletic representatives, and when so many millions of others see our representatives on television, being second rate is bad business. Some believe that at Wales we ran into bad luck. I say to you, no matter how you look at it, we simply seem to be bad; and what is more, we seem to be getting worse.
Mr. Andy O'Brien of Weekend magazine, the person who probably is best able to report on this sort of thing, has said that even in hockey, our best sport, he feels that our supremacy has not long to survive. Then in the gallery today there is Mr. Taylor, senior, who proceeded last year with the Kelowna team to Russia, and who I am sure was impressed with what he saw in that country in so far as athletic events were concerned.
In the first game there he saw the Canadian team go down to defeat before 17,000 Russian hockey fans by a score of 4 to 3. The press report said that the Russians outpaced and outskated the Canadians and generally out-shot them. In the second game there was a tie. In the third game there was a tie. In the last two games Canada was able to beat Russia. Bobbie Rosenfeld, the sports reporter, who was an outstanding Canadian athlete-in fact the outstanding Canadian athlete of the half century-stated:
We've been waiting desperately for something to cheer about ever since 1928 at Amsterdam-
Of course she was writing in 1952.
-when the lean and hungry looking Percy Williams popped the eyeballs out of the athletic world . . * We have been left wallowing in the wake of other more energetic nations who have become activated with the spirit of competition. Since the last Olympics, many countries, refusing the role of also-rans, have introduced development programs, with all athletes-junior and senior -tabbed. These countries have also set up a centralized coaching system which is most prominent in track and field and swimming.

She said that a survey should be made of Canada's athletic needs and problems and the talent available at the present time. She said also that we should have a development program. I should like to suggest that we get cracking and give our athletes an even break.
Then I noticed an article in the Canadian Commentator written by Mr. A. D. White, who is a popular and successful coach at the University of Toronto. Mr. White delivered a paper at the Couchiching conference and he said this when referring to the Olympic games:
It appears that in Canada there is little understanding of the professional calibre of this international sports show in which our athletes seem so poorly equipped to compete.
One interesting observation was this:
Some observers have interpreted our results at the games as an indication that the Canadian population is below par, physically.
If we are below par physically, Mr. Speaker, something ought to be done about it at an early date. I am sure all hon. members know the poem which goes like this:
But when that One Great Scorer comes to write against your name,
It's not whether you won or lost but how you played the game.
But as so many Canadians see it today, in international sport we have been become chronic good losers. There are too many Canadians, Mr. Speaker, who belong, I suggest, to the cult of "good losemanship". I am sure that all hon. members and for that matter ministers are tired of appeals being made to them for federal funds to assist travelling clubs. The creation of a Canada sports council would not end all the appeals, but at least the athletic governing bodies would be able to police themselves better and the essential things could be taken care of. That is what the Canada council has found to date. The council cannot take care of all appeals, but the essential things are taken care of.
Since last November I have received, as I imagine all hon. members have, letters from various athletic clubs throughout the country. There was an appeal made by the team that represented Canada in Moscow. In fact in connection with that appeal it looked just before they left as though they would not get sufficient money, and the officials were almost on the point of calling it off. We who live in the west witnessed the team having to go and play a number of exhibition games in order to raise funds, and one player remarked that the players were in a state of exhaustion before they ever left for overseas. I suggest that being in a state

Sports-Proposed Establishment of Council of exhaustion is no way to represent Canada before thousands of hockey fans overseas.
Then there was the appeal of the basketball team that represented Canada in Chile. That team, like all of the other clubs, received no federal assistance. However, that team put up a remarkable showing in Chile; it went on to beat Russia and defeated Mexico. I am sure that the Canadian team in Chile made a great number of friends there and did a great deal to help Canadian businessmen.
Then there was the appeal made by the grass hockey team that was to represent Canada in a series of games against England, Scotland, Ireland, Wales, Belgium, Denmark, Holland, Germany, France, United States and South Africa. The officials of that club felt that the federal government would want to assist these travelling ambassadors in cementing the healthy relations established during their last international conference.
Then there was a further appeal by the rugby team that is to represent Canada in Japan. The officials of that club have pointed out the numerous advantages of sending them as a truly representative team from Canada. We all know about the appeal for federal assistance for the Belleville McFarlands hockey team. We are all aware of the trouble the team officials had to go to in order to raise money to get to the Olympics. I do not need to deal with the troubles they had, but hon. members will recall that bingo games had to be staged and an agency apparently had to be appointed to assist.
Other countries have recognized the problem, Mr. Speaker, and action has been taken. I refer first of all to the United States. Public law 85-365 is an act to authorize certain activities by the armed forces in support of the 8th Olympic games and for other purposes. Section 2 of that act passed by the United States congress authorized certain things to be done, in addition to constructing on federal land in Squaw valley an arena suitable for the conduct of sports, and providing for appropriate ceremonies in connection with the 8th Olympic winter games. When completed the arena becomes the property of the United States. There was authorized by section 4 of the act a sum not to exceed $3,500,000.
Another United States public law was passed, No. 85-449, which was a joint resolution of the eighty-fifth congress, to authorize the designation of the week beginning October 3, 1958, as national Olympic week. Here the President of the United States was authorized to issue a proclamation designating the week to which I have referred as national Olympic week and urging all

citizens of that country to do all in their power to support the Olympic games, the Olympic winter games to be held in 1960, and the pan-American games to be held in 1959 at Chicago.
Then I notice, in making a review of the situation, that there were other public general bills of the United States. One, S-4038, authorizes the President to provide for tours of athletes from the United States to foreign countries, and to assist others in the United State. Then, as a matter of reference, there is another public law of the United States, No. 85-300, which authorizes construction, maintenance and operation by the armoury board in the district of Columbia in connection with the stadia in that district. It would appear that in the United States proclamations have been made almost annually by the president to assist amateur athletes in that country. I notice also, in making a review, that Russia, South American countries and England give much greater support to teams in international play and, as in the United States, the whole question of physical fitness is given active consideration.
Hon. members might like to know that in 1955 President Eisenhower called a White House conference to discuss the state of fitness of American youth. In 1956 the same president by executive order established the president's council on youth fitness, and in 1957 selected citizens were named to President Eisenhower's citizens' advisory committee. Other countries, Mr. Speaker, have realized that national prestige is increasingly associated with athletic showing.
Mr. Speaker, in order to assist all athletes, and at the same time improve the health of Canadians, I suggest the government should do the following. First, I think the Canada sports council should be established. Second, I feel that the government should request the council to survey the needs and basic requirements of our athletes. Third, I think the government should create a fund under the control of the council in the same way as with the Canada council, to assist amateur athletes. Fourth, I would suggest to the defence department that wherever and whenever possible this department should assist the amateurs.
Here, Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention that in the United States, for example, military transport will take athletes from all countries to the forthcoming pan-American games to be held in Chicago in August of this year, and return them free of charge by what is known as a friendship airlift. I understand, Mr. Speaker, that was inspired by the

U.S. state department. I suggest further that as the navy has to make trips to overseas ports, and as air transport has to make overseas trips, it might be feasible, say in 1960, to take such trips to Rome where the Olympic games will be held and transport the Canadian Olympic squad to that event.
Fifth, I would suggest that the government proclaim once every four years an Olympic week, when citizens can be urged to support with money the Canadian Olympic team. Sixth, the government should forthwith help the city of Vancouver or other cities of Canada which apply to hold the pan-American games. If Chile can entertain this large sports event, surely Canada can also. Vancouver at the moment is very interested, but Vancouver officials will say they cannot go it alone but need federal assistance.
I also noticed, in connection with the games to be held in Chicago, that the United States congress had passed a bill to help that city. I would urge that we also give every encouragement to the Canadian team representing this country at Chicago next year. I would suggest further that we send a large group; and possibly, if this council can be appointed, that they work out a Canada day in downtown Chicago. I am sure that many Canadians who now live in that city would enjoy seeing a Canada day there. It could be arranged, and it would be nice to show them that we still have something to cheer about in Canada.
Seventh, I suggest that on celebrating our centenary in 1967 a special effort be made to be host to the Olympic games that year. Ad-nittedly the games are to be held in 1968, but with an enthusiastic council possibly the Olympic committee could be persuaded to hold the games in 1967. Mr. Speaker, I suggest that anything is possible in connection with an event of this kind if we can get along with a Canada sports council.
Eighth, through the proposed council every assistance should be given to the hon. member for Calgary South, who is making such a wonderful effort to hold the winter Olympics at Banff in 1964 or 1968. Mr. McKay of that city and our colleague from Calgary South are doing a wonderful job for western Canada in this regard, and if they are able to hold the winter games at Banff it will do wonders for the whole of Canada. I believe it was that same combination that did so much to make the Grey cup classic what it is today.
There will be lasting benefits if Canada does hold the winter Olympics. One of them would surely be the reopening of the Banff Springs hotel. This, I suggest, would reverse the present trend of our skiing enthusiasts
proceeding to the great resorts in the United States, and would attract American skiing enthusiasts and tourists to Canada. The benefits in this regard would be enormous, and with a sports council recommendations can be made to handle this sort of thing.
In the Vancouver area, Mr. Speaker, it is the most amazing sight. We lack snow close to Vancouver, and upwards of 5,000 skiers will go every week to Mount Baker, some short distance south of the United States border. That is an area which has been developed by the United States federal government. It is an odd sight to see Canadians using those ski facilities and outnumbering the Americans by about three to one. With a sports council, new ideas can be put forward as to how we can develop our Canadian resorts and thereby give employment to many, many people. I notice that some 700 people will be employed at Squaw Valley next year when the Olympic games are held there. Certainly large numbers of people will be employed in the Banff area and throughout British Columbia for that matter, if we get the winter Olympics in 1964 or 1968.
Then I suggest, ninth, that a national school for coaches be established by the senior government through the Canada Council. I suggest that coaches properly trained could do so much with the young people of Canada. Here would be a national program aimed at the masses. The health of Canadian youth would improve, and from the many we could select more super athletes for international competition.
Tenth, the senior government in its national parks could give every consideration to the construction and erection of those things which would encourage the youth of Canada to participate in outdoor activities.
Eleventh, the senior government could work out a plan with the provincial governments, using the council, for a similar works project in provincial parks. Further, capital loans at low rates of interest could be made to resort owners willing to instal equipment to meet the demands of outdoor sportsmen.
I suggest that as many government departments would benefit by a program of this kind there would be no need to increase taxation in order to raise the funds that would be required under the Canada sports council. I suggest that there should be a reassessment of the entire situation. For one thing, a healthier nation would lead to a reduction in the need for hospital and medical services. For this reason the Department of National Health and Welfare should contribute to the Canada sports council fund. Then there are tremendous economic dividends when Canada does well in international

Sports-Proposed Establishment of Council play, and I suggest that the Department of Trade and Commerce be prepared to slice its budget in favour of making room for the Canada sports council. I do not know how many thousands of dollars they spent on the Brussells exhibit, but I suggest we spent little or nothing on such wonderful exhibits as Barbara Ann Scott, Anne Heggtveit of Ottawa and the Penticton V's. We spent little or nothing on the Penticton V's, yet this team thrilled all Canada and other countries besides. If the Department of Trade and Commerce appreciates all this, a contribution might well be made.
I suggest also that there might be a reassessment with respect to the national film board. I notice that this year 43 films in 15 languages were completed for distribution. As Canadian athletes do the same job, namely the job of selling Canada, surely it would be wise to permit a budget cut here in favour of the sports council. I feel also that a healthy contribution should be made by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I suggest that a healthy council, properly endowed, might stop the decay of the muscle of our youth and reverse the trend, allowing us to keep up with the athletic advancement of other nations.
I think generally speaking we have treated our travelling ambassadors poorly. They go overseas badly equipped. They need much more in the way of suitable dress. I wish to compliment the officials and sponsors of clubs who do send these travelling ambassadors overseas, and I can hardly criticize them for doing a little bit of advertising on the side, but it is confusing to many sports fans overseas to see a maple leaf on the front of a sweater and find some advertising material on the back. I think in time this situation may get worse unless some federal assistance is forthcoming. It may well come to pass that we shall see such a sign as "Ace Beer" on the front of a sweater and "Acme Moving Company" on the back.
We must give more financial assistance to these clubs; otherwise they may well be forced to advertise. We do make blazers available from time to time, but if it is a rainy day blazers cannot be worn, and the athletes have no windbreakers or jackets to wear in substitution. Our sportsmen abroad often lack the means of exchanging the common courtesies. Most other clubs taking part in international competitions are able to supply what are called traders. They give away badges, pins, miniature flags and so on. However, our teams go overseas without that sort of thing, and many of our officials are embarrassed when we are on the receiving end and are not able to give such things in exchange.
	,
Mr. Speaker, my time must be running out. In closing, may I say that I feel we should appoint this sports council and then go all out to celebrate Canada's centenary in 1967. I suggest that at an early date through the sports council we petition the pan-American games committee to have this great event here in 1967. As the Olympic games are to be held the following year, possibly the same plant and equipment could be used for both events. I suggest we tie in an athletic spectacle with a world's fair for Canada.
Here in Ottawa surely, as we are celebrating Canada's birthday, we might well be the centre of a great birthday party. The city certainly needs a larger and more modern sports field to hold national and international events. If a stadium could be constructed here for great national classics it might well be that the Grey cup game could be played in Ottawa in 1967.
These are some of the things that could be considered if we did get the type of man I have suggested on the sports council; and if it was properly endowed with funds that council would be able to do wonders for Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a few words in support of the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor). There is no doubt that the motion has much merit, for Canadian amateur sport seems to be somewhat on the wane. In the smaller communities, it is even difficult to keep it going at all. However, I cannot fully agree with the hon. member's suggestion that what is needed is a Canada sports council along the lines of the Canada arts council. In my view, there is an enormous difference between arts, public education, and sports.
Of course, I do not claim that sports should be neglected; on the contrary, to my mind, they should receive federal support. Our teams do not rank as highly as they should at Olympic or Commonwealth games because our sports organizations are not strong enough to enable players to train without holding a paying job somewhere, and are thus prevented from adequate, thorough training.
That is why I feel that the Canadian government should consider the advisability of setting up a Canada sports council to support amateur sport. However, I do not share the hon. member for Vancouver-Bur-rard's suggestions in regard to some persons who should be made members of the Canada sports council.

The hon. member seems to favour the appointment of certain professional sport magnates and promoters; that is exactly what is wrong with sports in Canada.
Professional sport magnates in Canada have such a grip on sports that they paralyse all amateur sports not under their control. In the field of sports Canada is faced with a certain form of slavery, due to Canadian professional sports magnates.
I could give several examples, but shall mention only two. Take the case of the "Canadiens" hockey team, whose directors have been unwilling for over three years to grant amateur status to a member of the team who has refused to be "demoted" to the "Royals", although amateur status would have enabled him to play in a lesser league in the area. In fact, he was to have joined the Hull Legion team. This he was not allowed to do because he had refused to play on a minor league team when he was the property of the "Canadiens". He was also prevented from playing on the Belleville team, which will be taking part in amateur competitions in Europe.
The same situation occurred in Toronto. An 18-year old student who had signed a contract with the Toronto team, was barred from playing organized hockey, for having made some unfortunate remarks about Mr. Connie Smythe; the latter decided that he would never be allowed to play in organized hockey. That young man was unable to play, much as he tried to get permission.
It is therefore necessary that the Canada sports council be empowered to reverse the decision of this dangerous organization of professional sports magnates, so that amateurs may, after playing for a season on a particular team, or having fulfilled a contract for a season or two, decide on the type of game they wish to play and choose the team they prefer to play on.
These are further reasons, Mr. Speaker, why we should establish a Canada sports council. That is also why I urge the government, if the proposal is carried, to see that professional sports magnates be kept out of this council, because they are the bane of amateur sports.
I therefore hope, Mr. Speaker, that the government will consider my remarks if ever the sports council is set up.

Mr. Speaker, one of the leading Brahmins of the world of culture, T. S. Elliot, wrote a book sometime

Events such as the cup final and the annual Oxford and Cambridge rugby classic were very much to the fore in his remarks on English culture in that book. If we look at the United States scene we can see that such national events as the Kentucky derby and the world series are a strong indication that sports have permeated their culture very deeply, and sports is a subject worthy of consideration in any national assembly.
What I wish to do in my remarks today is trace something of the history of sporting developments in Canada. speechtext:
One of the ideas implicit in the hon. member's resolution is that Canada must attain some status in the international field of sports and since sports have become a means by which a nation attains international status and recognition Canada has to get into the picture. Canadians suffer from a great inferiority complex toward the United States in the field of sports and we would have to overcome this. At one time back in the golden age of Canadian sports between 1870 and 1905 we did not have to take a back seat to the United States and as a matter of fact we were held up to them as an example. To illustrate this I have here a little poem written back in 1877 to commemorate the feats of Ned Hanlan who went to the Philadelphia centennial sporting events and then to
1044	HOUSE OF
Sports-Proposed Establishment of Council England where he distinguished himself. The poem is entitled "The Ode" and reads as follows:
Hail to the champion sculler,
Toronto's manly son.
Who, across the line and on the Tyne Hath famous victories won.
And with three cheers for Hanlan,
The champion of the oar,
Let us shout, hurrah for Canada!
The land which such hero bore.
It is lousy poetry but the point is that it expresses the national sentiment that is involved in the hon. member's resolution. There have been a great many silly things attributed to sports in Canada. One myth that is encountered on the sports page of almost any newspaper from time to time is that lacrosse is the national game of Canada. According to some accounts an act of this house was passed on July 1, 1867 making lacrosse our national game. That happens to be a pack of nonsense but no one has ever explored the question in an effort to understand how the idea developed. Lacrosse is one of the most fascinating examples of what happens to sports in Canada.
I suggest that if you look into the history of sports and games in this country you will find they never developed from the play of children but always from a situation wherein people had leisure time, sufficient money and adequate status in a community to organize the game on a fine, rational basis. Dr. W. G. Beers, the man who codified the rules of lacrosse and is responsible for the myth that it is our national game, is an example of this. He was a fairly well-to-do dentist in Montreal and consorted with people such as the Abbotts and Redpaths who were well-known in Montreal sporting and moneyed circles. A small group of such young men connected with McGill University had watched Indians play lacrosse and decided that it was an attractive game. They rationalized and adapted the sport and developed a code of rules. With the coming of confederation Beers decided to tie the two developments together and so he hammered across the idea that on July 1, 1867 we would have a new national game as well as a new nation. Thus the idea was born and lacrosse ever since has been referred to as our national sport because of this publicity. Of course, it has never really been an official game. You cannot find it mentioned anywhere in the statutes or in an order in council. As a matter of fact, on July 1, 1867, the day on which it was supposed to have been made our national sport, the House of Commons, although it sat, did not have any discussion or debate nor did it take up any business in which such a step could have been taken. 

As a game, lacrosse went through a period of tremendous expansion and in that expansion it manifested one of the prominent tendencies of sports in Canada. The local towns, small cities and larger centres all want to get into the game and they do so with great local pride once they become established in the sport. That happened with lacrosse, football and hockey. They quickly moved across the country. In each case the people wanted to have a national championship. As a matter of fact, within two years of the C.P.R. reaching the west coast the people in that area were sending down a lacrosse team in an effort to capture the national award.
The trend to group participation in national sporting games has been extremely strong in Canada. In one period we had people like Mr. P. D. Ross, publisher of the Ottawa Journal, and "Iron" Mike Fallon, later bishop of London, who was the first man to introduce American football ideas into Canadian football in the 1890's. There was a great sporting fervour at that time.
If you analyse the reason for this infectious interest in sport which existed at that time it was because these sports were in the hands of a fairly small group of people who had leisure and a certain amount of money. This accounted for the expansion. Eventually, professionalism entered the scene in Canada although there were early glimmerings of it before 1867 and certainly Ned Hanlan is reported to have made $85,000 in one expedition. However, professionalism in the true sense did not enter the picture until 1907 when a football coach for the first time was paid a salary. His name was Chauncey Elliott. The next year and the next, lacrosse, which had been semi-professional but largely amateur, became professional in the full sense and then a professional hockey league came into being.
With the development of professionalism in Canada, paralleled by developments in the United States, you had a different type of conflict in the athletic scene than you had ever had before. A very famous Spanish philosopher, Ortega y Gasset, has put the whole basis of our society as having developed out of a game and a subsequent code of rules. His argument was that the British had the best democratic sense in the whole world because they had developed this idea of gamesmanship, not in the Stephen Potter sense, but in the sense of respect for the game to the point where they played it as gentlemen, and while the idea of winning was usually paramount it never got in the way of the fact that they wanted to have a good game. So you got this code of ethics and sense of fairness, and English gentlemen, coming out

of schools such as Eton, Winchester and the rest, carried this into their parliamentary life and helped to give it stability and a fair code that many of the other countries of the world have never been able to match.
So far as politics are concerned, I have noticed that politicians cannot stay away from sport. In one of this first ambits or gambits after being elected, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) appeared, very athletically clad, to kick the football at a Grey cup match. We can all remember the late Mr. King prancing out when Barbara Ann Scott came home in order to benefit from her publicity. He was seen with her on several occasions. I think that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) has been able to make a great play out of the fact that he *was a good athlete, that he is a very sporting type and can talk the language of sport. To me, perhaps the most amusing incident in the political scene had to do with a C.C.F. member. I remember how stunned I was when I saw the former member for Winnipeg North Centre cavorting around at Grey cup time with a sombrero on his head.
The theme of the athlete and the game being important in national terms is something that has been close to us for a very long time, and it seems to me that the decision we have to face is whether we actually want to subsidize sport under the international conditions that exist today. A number of members of our group are in favour of the motion in principle. I would abstain from voting on it because I feel that the conditions attached to the resolution by the member who introduced it largely represent things that I cannot support.
Games, sports, athletics, whatever you want to call them, amateur or professional, games of skill, games of chance, represent a very cluttered and mixed up situation when we consider them and try to decide whether they are worth while or not worth while. I know one of the causes of the split in our views. It can be seen in a number of historical references. I remember reading about the villages and towns of Nova Scotia. It was said that in villages where the Baptist or Methodist churches were strong they never had many sporting events whereas if you had a lot of Anglicans sport flourished. It can also be said that the Irish Catholics introduced many phases of sport into Canada. They came from Boston to St. Michaels' College and the University of Ottawa and gave Canadian sport its biggest boost in the 1880's and 1890's. Several players from the St. Michaels' College baseball team went right into the professional leagues. One of Canada's first wealthy men, a Torontonian,
Sports-Proposed Establishment of Council was the only Canadian I know of who ever owned a major league baseball team. Unfortunately it was the New York Yankees in the days before they were the New York Yankees so he did not do very well.
To come back to the contribution of the Irish Catholics, not only do we see it in the United States in the case of universities like Notre Dame but we can also see it in Canada in the case of St. Michaels' College. In contrast, I was intrigued by a book issued about 1905 having to do with French Canadian athletes and heroes. There was only one person mentioned who played a team game. That was Nap Lajoie, a resident of the United States of French Canadian origin. Mention was made of strong men such as Louis Cyr or strong women or boxers or wrestlers which indicated that for many years French Canadians stayed away from team games. They were never encouraged to go into them. Their basic physical strength and prowess at sport and at hard work led them into the weight lifting and wrestling fields. From about 1910 on you can see the beginning of French Canadian names creeping more and more into lacrosse and hockey line-ups until today, as all hon. members know, some of us from Ontario feel that they rather dominate the game of hockey.
Contributions have been made by other national groups. If any of you come from Kitchener you will be aware of what the Germans gave to Canada through gymnastics and the turnerbunds they introduced. The Caledonian games, which have been taking place in Ontario for seventy to eighty years, have been to a greater or lesser degree a contribution to athletics and to the development of strength in tossing the caber. I feel that such contributions have meant a great deal to the colour and tone of Canadian life. The Guelph Maple Leafs, for example, put Guelph on the map long before George Drew entered the house as leader of the opposition. Away back in the 1870's the Guelph Maple Leafs were North American baseball champions.
I am giving a number of these examples to try to show that sport has always been a very large part of the Canadian social life and social scene. Within two years of confederation two teams raised enough money through personal subscriptions to make tours of England in order to play cricket and lacrosse. Throughout the 1880's and 1890's and up to the advent of professionalism almost every year some team of some kind or other went over to Great Britain or down into the United States to demonstrate their prowess.

Sports-Proposed Establishment of Council From the reading I have done I cannot remember, however, that there were ever any demands that these teams be supported by the government.
Some of you must remember the discussion last year when Great Britain challenged the United States for the American cup. It was mentioned that Canada had twice done so. In 1873 the ship, Countess of Dufferin, named for the wife of the governor general at that time, entered the race and made a very poor showing, such a showing that editorials were written in all Canadian newspapers lamenting this disgrace, but in none of these editorials was there any demand that the government should step in and put up a sum of money in order to produce a better boat.
The very fact that such a resolution as this is introduced by a member of a party that has "Conservative" in its title throws some light upon the changing times. While we know that the hon. member introduced certain caveats about not letting the state go too far, in effect what he is asking for was subsidization, even for his own beautiful city of Vancouver so that they can put on a big show. This puts us over a watershed of some kind or other. I hope that if members of his party speak in support of the resolution and later vote for it they will realize that their claim to the title "Conservative" is going to go by the boards.
There is one authority in Canada today to whom I should like to refer. At least, I feel he is an authority although he has been much maligned. I refer to Lloyd Percival who made sports college very well known. A number of years ago I took up with him the question of what he thought we should do in the international field. I asked him this question:
What ideas or opinions have you on the efforts Canada should make in the field of international sport, for example, at the Olympic games?
His answer was:
I believe that if Canada is going to take part in national sport especially at the Olympic games and British Empire games that the country should make an organized effort to develop adequate representation.
By adequate, I mean both in ability and attitude. The first step it seems to me is to develop an Olympic awareness amongst our youth. Here in Canada there are only comparatively few who ever think in their youth of the great honour of representing their country at the Olympic games. In other countries this is a major job to a large proportion of the athletic population. Following this, of course, there must be developed a scheme for improved coaching and facilities. This could well be the subject for a book.
Later on, I asked him this:
If Canada should make a planned and serious try for international laurels in Olympic events, do you think government sponsorship is necessary, in whole or in part?

The answer was:
Yes, I believe that government sponsorship is very necessary if Canada is to do anything about improving our international reputation in athletics. I believe a development committee should be set up to handle the financial support provided by the government. On this development committee should be representatives from all those activities concerned.
Now, when I suggested that I would give partial support to this resolution, I meant in this particular field of athletics only and not that I felt any team games, like hockey or football, should be given support. No such team in Canada at the present time deserves any government support for its present activities. When I think of the Belleville McFarlands going to Britain and touring Europe under the tender guidance of that British bandit Bunny Ahearne, I lose sympathy for them. I lived for several years in England and I associated with hockey players there. My sympathy for the Belleville McFarlands went out the window because I know that the Canadian amateur hockey association

do they still claim to be amateurs?; I am not sure because I have lost track of these things-has a good deal of money in the bank and can do fairly well in its organizational aspects in the playoffs toward getting money for this sort of thing. If they are the national governing body that supports hockey in this country, then surely it is their responsibility to send a representative team abroad.
It is easy enough to say that the Russians are in effect pros, supported by the government. What is wrong with that? Our sham amateurs cannot say there is anything wrong with it. However, in this particular regard, I feel this is one of the phases that no government should be called upon to support. The same remarks will apply to almost any other team game of which one can think.
One of the reasons why professionalism has tended to destroy Canada's participation in international athletic events is that it offers very glistening opportunities to young people for this kind of hard work as compared to track and field events. One of the goals of most of the young men in the particular community from which I come is to become a professional hockey player. I believe there are 50 or 60 men from the lakehead community making a living in hockey at the present time. This incentive or this particular goal has led to a concentration by our young men who have athletic ability into this more rewarding field of sport. There is nothing wrong with that but it explains why we are not competing in international track and field events. They are not attractive enough to our young people.

One of the other reasons is that there is a social change taking place. Any teacher will tell you that we have backed down the male-female relationship to the ages of 12 and 13. I think anyone who has coached these team games realizes that a lot of boys begin to drop out of hockey or other team sports at 14 or 15. The boys find that the intensive activity which football or other sports demand, as well as the demands on their school time, do not comport very well with their social life when they are in the boy-girl stage. Sport is one of the things that suffers.
In relation to the National Physical Fitness Act, I may say that in 1954 the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) buried this act. As I remember from scanning through the debates that occurred there was no one from the Progressive Conservative party who stood up and tried to keep it going. I should like to point out some of the aims of that act to the hon. member who introduced this resolution. Section 4 of the act, subsection (b) says:
(b) encourage, develop and correlate all activities relating to physical development of the people through sports, athletic and other similar pursuits;
Some $225,000 annually was set aside by the federal government to be distributed to the provinces on a pro rata basis if they would undertake to use the money for the purposes set out in this act. The reason for the introduction of the act was that most Canadians were amazed and alarmed at the state of the physical fitness of our young people when they were called up for the armed services. As a consequence of that concern this act was passed. In the 10 years that the act was in force the full grant was never taken. As a matter of fact, only a couple of provinces, I believe British Columbia and Saskatchewan, took any real interest in it, although Nova Scotia and Ontario did make some efforts.
The point I should like to make with the hon. member is that we had a piece of legislation on the statute books for 10 years and it was allowed to die in this House of Commons without anyone defending it. This legislation, essentially, would have done exactly what the sponsor of this resolution wants. It seems to me that the passing away of this act should make us ask the question, is this the sort of field into which we want to go?
I cannot find a bit of information for which I was looking, Mr. Speaker, but it had to do with a statement made by Dr. W. C. Ross of Nova Scotia, who was one of the members of the national physical fitness council set up under this legislation that the Hon. Ian Mackenzie introduced during the war years.
Sports-Proposed Establishment of Council Dr. Ross stressed almost the same thing that the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) stressed, that we should be very careful in using federal funds to distinguish sharply between professionalism and amateurism. The very idea of an amateur is one who loves the sport or game and not the personal gain from it.
In the main, this legislation was really a tremendous failure. If you go across the country and talk to men who were active in physical education in the university faculties or in provincial health departments, I think you will find that they feel the government lost its enthusiasm for the act and the people seemed to lose their enthusiasm for it. There is another example of a particular act in the provincial field. The premier of Ontario introduced a community arena program with provincial subsidization. I think that across Ontario today many of these community arena projects are recognized as being relatively white elephants compared to the success that was hoped for them.
The conclusion to which anyone who is close to sport or has been close to it in any way must come is that it is a rather phony kind of atmosphere today in its higher levels. I have no particular complaint and I do not think any member of this house has, but there is much more space and time in the writing field devoted to covering professional hockey and football than to say professional politics. This happens to be the situation and the emphasis has always been intensifying on the personality, on the big hero.
In recent years we seem to have lost the conception of a game as something that enabled us to lose ourselves, to escape from time, and by means of which we learned coordination and co-operation almost instinctively. The idea of the game itself being important has gone, and the emphasis now is on some Mr. Big who happens to score three goals or some pitcher who happens to have his arm in good shape or Mr. Bernie Faloney who happens to throw clusters of successful passes in a day. You no longer get the emphasis upon the game as the thing in itself.
I do not particularly regret this tendency but a concentration that focuses publicity upon the big-timers in any particular sport again undermines the whole idea of amateur games and any sort of efforts on a national and an international level in the fields such as track and field that do not bring in the rewards. I think many hon. members have noticed the pressures that the sensational Australian Herb Elliott has been under to get him to turn professional. There is the promoter

Our United States friends, despite what was read by the hon. member who introduced this resolution, have not really gone as far as he would have suggested in supporting international competition. There has been tremendous demand for such aid to sport and wherever there has been any kind of loophole they have tended to use that loophole. But in the main the United States has ignored it, as any hon. members who have read Avery Brundage will have found out. He has been the leading figure in the United States Olympic program. The Americans have never really had substantial government support. I would put this up to the Progressive Conservative member. One of the reasons they have not had it is that they felt it introduced a conflict between the conception they tend to talk so much about, namely free enterprise, and sport they feel would suffer if it had government subsidies.
In closing my remarks I wanted at least to give them a slight humorous pitch. I wanted to read something written about 350 years ago about the virtue of a certain game, namely the game of football. While it has its humorous aspect, I think it is still one of the fundamental reasons why we should be interested in cultivating sport on a much more common denominator, that is on a mass basis. This was written by an Elizabethan educationist, Richard Mulcaster, and he said this:
If well played . . . football strengthened and brawneth the whole body and by provoking superfluities downward, it dischargeth the head, and upper partes, it is good for the bowells and to drive down the stone and graven from both the bladder and kidnies. It helpeth weak hammes, by much moving . . . thickening the flesh no lesse than riding doth.
Three hundred and fifty years ago this educator could see the value of football. I want to contrast that particular point of view with another quotation written by a modern-day psychoanalyst who looked at the sport of football as a psychoanalyst. He said:
-in psychoanalytic language the football will be for the rugby enthusiast the symbol of maternal images, objects of love; for the soccer player, a symbol of paternal virility which is not a little awesome and demands special forms of taboo or control.
We get into by-channels of this kind today when we begin to analyse sport too closely. There are thousands of books turned out by Americans within the last few years about this social phenomenon of sport, the whole idea of mass sport.
In closing, I should like to indicate to the hon. member who introduced this resolution the idea that there is a confusion in his mind

as to what he really wants in terms of government support. I do not think he really wants our government supporting teams to go abroad or to take part in activities with our American friends or even within the country, who are able to charge at the gate and get any kind of return, or in other words who can put their operations on a professional basis.
Read the resolution. It refers to amateur sport definitely.

My colleague has referred me to the word "amateur". I should like him to define that word "amateur". We have a Canadian hockey association which is amateur and yet almost all the players in it are professional, that is once you get up to the junior level. The whole question of amateur versus professional was talked out in Canada from about 1910 to the 1930's when a sort of Victorian purity began to operate in matters of athletics and we had people banned from playing. If they were professional football players they were not allowed to play amateur hockey and so on. Hon. members will all recall that the famous cult of amateurism really developed out of English rowing activities where an amateur was defined as someone who did not work with his hands. One Canadian who went over to England and challenged in the field of rowing was not given the opportunity to compete because he worked with his hands. The same thing happened to the United States rower, a man by the name of Kelly, who I believe has some offspring now, a princess in Monaco.
But in defending myself from this charge of not reading the resolution addressed to me by my compatriot here, I have wandered somewhat away from the topic under discussion. I should just like to say that I would not support the resolution although parts of it are fairly good. I think the intention all the way through perhaps has been good. However, I would abstain from voting.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate I would first congratulate the mover of this resolution, the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor), on the initiative he has shown in bringing this resolution before us, the hard work which he has done in preparing the address which was delivered today and also on the contribution which that hon. gentleman has made over the years to Canadian sport. In this past 18 months I have had the privilege of being deskmate and roommate of the hon. member

for Vancouver-Burrard and I know something of his sincerity in this matter of promoting athletics in Canada. I would also refer at this time to the father of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, namely Mr. Fred "Cyclone" Taylor whose name when I was a child was a household word in sports-minded households, and who will go down in history as one of the great Canadian athletes of all time.
I was pleased that the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) concluded what he had to say with what he termed a slight humorous pitch. In my view there is nothing at all humorous about the references which he made near the beginning of his address to two Canadian citizens who have contributed so much to the game of hockey in this country. Whether or not what he said about those people is true, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to him that it ill behooves a member of parliament to malign in the way he did two individual Canadian citizens who are not here and therefore are unable to reply to him. But on their behalf and, of course, without their authority, I respectfully suggest to him that what he said is completely untrue.
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to what the hon. member had to say in his rambling address. In the very short time I have been here I have become quite fond of the hon. member for Port Arthur. I admire him as a distinguished teacher and a conscientious member of parliament. But I must say that I had some difficulty half way through his speech in trying to decide whether or not he supported this resolution. It seemed to him a bad thing that Conservative members would be bold enough to suggest that sport be subsidized in the way it is proposed this Canada sports council be supported by federal funds. It seems to me that the hon. member really failed to hear what the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard had to say because, in essence, what he proposed was modest federal government support in a financial way of athletics in this country with a view to raising the standards of athletic achievement, and with a view to giving financial support to meet the expenses of amateur Canadians competing in international competition abroad. That is the essence of this resolution, as I understand it, and that is the resolution which I hope all hon. members will support at the conclusion of this debate.
Mr. Speaker, during these past few days when this resolution has been under discussion around the House of Commons I have been impressed by the unanimous support which it has attracted on all sides of the house. I am hoping that later today we will
Sports-Proposed Establishment of Council hear from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) who, according to legend, was a semi-professional ball player at one time, and who is still seen at least once a year playing ball on the lawn of parliament hill.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that federal action of the kind the hon. member has proposed is something we should support for very good reasons. I think there is growing circumstantial evidence that Canadians generally are less physically fit than people in many other countries. I say "circumstantial evidence", because there have been no adequate tests carried out by competent people across the nation upon which we could come to a definite conclusion in this regard. However, as I say, there is evidence that Canadians generally are less physically fit than many people from other countries both in Europe and Asia. I think one piece of evidence is that, with isolated exceptions, Canadians have a bad record in international competition. At the last Olympic games in 1956 Canada, in unofficial standings, finished seventeenth, behind such small countries as Hungary, Korea and Iran. It seems to me that in a country endowed as this one is with great resources, a standard of living second only to that of the United States, with magnificent climate, and so many other physical amenities, it is simply a national disgrace that in 1956 we send a team to the Olympics which winds up seventeenth. I also say it is a national disgrace that up until this time there has been so little done on the part of the parliament of Canada to promote, sponsor and assist our athletes who compete in international competitions.
Of course, there have been exceptions to this general rule. Percy Williams, the famous sprinter, first brought renown to Canada in his success in the 1928 Olympics. Barbara Ann Scott, Marlene Stewart Streit, Doug Hepburn of Vancouver, Barbara Wagner, Bob Paul of Toronto and Ann Heggtveit of this city, all of these great athletes have brought honour to Canada, in many cases in spite of the lack of encouragement and support from any government in this country.
Mr. Speaker, there are many examples of Canadians going to the Olympics and other international athletic games ill prepared and ill equipped. I happen to know something about the team that represented Canada in yachting in the last two Olympic games, and I am told that when our sailors got there in the 1948 games, in the Star class they found their gear, equipment and boat were just not really fit to compete successfully against the equipment and yachts that the European and other competitors had. Notwithstanding this lack of financial support, the yachting fraternity in this country have been busy

Sports-Proposed Establishment of Council since 1956 promoting the sport and raising money on their own. In this connection much credit lor the success which I am sure we are going to have at the next Olympics in yachting must go to Ray Engholm, president of the Canadian yachting association, Bill Gooderham, who will probably compete for Canada at the next Olympic games, and Paul Phelan, the vice-president for Ontario of the Canadian yachting association.
Mr. Speaker, another fact which indicates that Canadians are less physically fit than the people in other parts of the world is the high rate of rejections for the armed services. Figures in this regard are not available in this country, but studies of rejections for the armed services of the United States indicate that there is a higher rate in the services of that country than in European armies. I suggest that social and economic conditions in the United States are very similar to those which obtain in this country, and therefore a similar condition exists here. There have been many accurate and authentic studies made in the United States in this field. In 1955 it was reported to the President of the United States by the sports governing bodies of that country that 78.3 per cent of children tested-and they tested a sample of American children-could not pass the minimum muscular fitness test which is used in testing patients before they are discharged from physiotherapy clinics. Of a comparable group of European children who were tested, only 8.5 per cent failed to qualify.
A further little piece of evidence came to light recently in the report of the director of programs for the girl scouts of America who reported that in her opinion American girls do not have the same energy for hiking or folk dancing or other similar athletic endeavours as do European girls of the same age. I think the reason for this state of affairs in this country and in the United States is quite obvious. In North America we are becoming soft and flabby. We seldom think of walking; we always drive. Last night I attended a cocktail party in Toronto, and three people who came from a house not seven houses away from the place where this party was being held drove their cars to the party.
We have become, or we are fast becoming, it is fair to say, a nation of spectators instead of participants-and how soon this unfortunate characteristic becomes evident to us. On Sunday morning I walked into my living room at nine o'clock and there were three bodies-the bodies of my three children-on the floor watching the television, and only the most severe kind of prodding could get them out of the living room and on their way to Sunday school at ten o'clock. I must say

in their defence that one of them is a hockey player, when he is not watching television, playing for two teams; the other is a swimmer and the third, I hope, will be a politician.
Three sportsmen.
Out of order: that is not an amateur sport.

Another interesting condition of affairs is that it is no longer fashionable in this country-and everybody these days tries to do the things that are fashionable- to engage in sports which require great stamina and endurance. I think hon. members will find that very few people after they have passed the age of adolescence become seriously interested in personal participation in track and field athletic activities, for instance.
The advantages of raising the physical fitness of Canadians are of course quite plain. People who are healthy, fit and vigorous work better and think better. With increasing standards of physical health fewer people will go to hospital and more will be able to remain full time at their daily work. The loss of earnings attributable to sickness in this country must be truly fantastic, to say nothing of the anguish and concern which is caused in a family when the head of a family is ill and unable to work. It is quite obvious, also, that athletic programs could help children by preventing them from joining street gangs or seeking cheap thrills and belonging to that well known class of adolescents called juvenile delinquents.
There is a further reason I would put forward for supporting this resolution, and it is this; there is no doubt at all that success in athletics and games would add greatly to our national prestige abroad. There is little doubt in my mind that the peoples of Asia and eastern Europe must be disappointed in this country when their athletes go to international athletic contests and find Canadians doing as poorly as they have done in recent international events. The peoples of those countries respect and admire physical vigour, endurance, stamina and athletic excellence.
So, Mr. Speaker, it is with great enthusiasm that I support the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. In my opinion the council should be comprised of some 25 people appointed by the governor in council, one from each of the 25 sports governing bodies in Canada. I suggest that initially this body should be supported by a federal government grant of $100,000 a year. The national ballet is now receiving from the Canada Council an annual grant of $75,000, and if the taxpayers of this country can pay $75,000 to the ballet-a payment

which, by the way, I believe to be justified -then surely $100,000 a year could be found for sport. I hope that one of the functions of this sports council would be to encourage benefactions from citizens and sports minded people across the country. I hope that people would be encouraged to leave bequests to this council and that it would also receive donations from amateur and professional athletic organizations. It seems to me that this council could play a large part in raising the physical fitness of the Canadian people, in co-ordinating the activities of the sports governing bodies of Canada and in promoting the participation of Canadian teams in international competitions. I hope all members of this house will approve this resolution and, on its being passed, will have some part to play in helping the Canada sports council to become a successful agency of the government.

Mr. Speaker, I should make my position very clear at the outset as far as this motion is concerned. I support it 100 per cent. I think it is an excellent motion, and it should not only receive the support of all hon. members but everyone should, in his own conscience, decide that it is not going to be talked out tonight but that it shall come to a vote. For this reason I do not intend to speak at great length.
Along with other hon. members I listened with a great deal of respect to some of the opinions expressed by my colleague from Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), but I think this is one of the occasions when we can agree in principle but differ with respect to application. As far as I am concerned I take the view that whether a person is wealthy or a pauper he needs good health. Whether he is subnormal in intelligence or a genius he cannot go very far without good health. It is a matter of the utmost importance to all of us here, as legislators in the national field, that the people of this country should be as healthy as it is possible for them to be. I know very well that a few years ago we enacted the federal physical act. It had a short life and therefore an early death. But that does not detract from the fact that it was a good idea.
If in the history of mankind when a new idea apparently died we did not try to reincarnate it, reestablish it and resuscitate it we would be back in the age of barbarism. When a good and fresh idea unfortunately fails that does not deter us trying to revive the basic principle and underlying thought perhaps in some new form. The physical fitness program inaugurated by the federal government several years ago represented

In the province of British Columbia only a few years ago a wonderful experiment in the field of physical fitness was introduced under the brilliant leadership of the Hon.
G.	M. Weir and the Hon. George Pearson. We had established there a challenging program of physical fitness under which thousands of children and adults in the province received training in gymnastics and physical culture under supervision. It is one of the most marvelous programs in this field about which I have heard. For some reason I do not understand the present government of British Columbia discontinued the program which was a disgraceful action. It is my hope that the spirit of the resolution before us will come into reality in the establishment of a council such as is suggested which will set up a minimum basis of physical education and amateur sport activity.
We in this group supported the establishment of the Canada Council for culture in the arts which was a good measure but having such a council cannot mean very much if people have not the state of good health to permit their taking advantage of it. I therefore believe that the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (M. Taylor) is the necessary adjunct, corollary or partner to the Canada Council for culture in the arts. If the Canadian parliament was prepared to establish and finance a council for culture in the arts there can be no reasonable argument against establishing and financing a council for physical fitness and amateur sports. If you support the one you must support the other.
I believe there is another important aspect of this question. The position of Canada must be defined with respect to sending our basketball, football, hockey, swimming and other contestants to international meets. Every time a Canadian team is about to go abroad the sponsor must practically get down on his hands and knees to beg from individuals and companies sufficient moneys to finance the trip. Scarcely a day or week goes by but that businessmen, corporations and members of parliament receive requests for money and if you do not kick through you are a dirty you-know-what. That is not good for morale in sports or for the morale of the contestants. I am not going to mention names but I shall give an illustration.
