Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor) for his fine speech. I am very happy to see his well-known father in the gallery.
Today's youth, our most precious heritage, are striving for things in life that appear most important to them and which will eventually bring success in future years. My connections with sports for over 35 years and my overseas and other experience in this old world of ours have given me much food for thought. I sincerely believe that the three greatest assets of our youth would be Christian training, education and recreation. Give me the boy or girl who will combine those three and I am sure we would never have to worry about juvenile delinquency.
[Mr. Winch.)

Speaking today in support of the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard I should like to relate my remarks to one of these great assets, recreation. Recreation builds healthy bodies and minds. Indeed, it benefits the physical and mental development of those participating. Last but not least, it provides good sportsmanship, fellowship and friendship and perhaps the greatest of these would be friendship.
The poem, "Making Friends", supports my statement:
Life is sweet not because of the things we do
But the things in common we share.
We want to live on not because of ourselves
But because of the people who care.
It's giving and doing for somebody else.
On that all life's splendour depends.
For the joy of the world when you've summed it all up
Is found in the making of friends.
I believe that the boy or girl who participates in some form of recreation will become a better citizen of this great country of ours. The fine assistance of many organizations, including the Canadian sports advisory council, the Canadian amateur hockey association, the Canadian Legion with its youth training plan, in an effort to upgrade the standard of Canadian track and field athletics and the individual efforts of our coaches, managers and executive members have given our youth greater opportunities in recreational participation. Through the efforts of many sports minded citizens, arenas, community centres and stadiums have been built almost overnight.
The value of these buildings cannot be estimated in dollars and cents. Yes, I know that some people will argue that the cost of these structures is prohibitive and the upkeep too great, but I sincerely believe that if we can keep one boy from going to Guelph reformatory or some similar institution the investment is more than worth while because, after all, that boy could be your boy or mine. Today it costs about $150 to equip a boy for most sports, but let me bring to your attention the fact that if that boy should go wrong it would cost $2,000 or more to send him to some penal institution.
In my remarks up to the present, Mr. Speaker, I have mentioned the value of recreation. I am sure that you will agree with me that there is a great need for a sports training program in the dominion of Canada on a national scale in order that we can compete favourably with other countries. Sports organizations throughout our country have dedicated their time and effort toward this great cause but lack of finances have stifled their efforts. Government financial

assistance, along with the outstanding spirit of these organizations and individuals, could bring splendid results.
Since I spoke in parliament recently on government assistance to sports and hinted that possibly a ministry of sports and athletic development might be the answer, I have been assured of the wholehearted support of many sports leaders. While the press has greeted the idea with mixed feelings, everything indicates that the mass of the people who are involved in sports in any capacity are in favour of the idea in principle. Working out details is a problem but certainly not an insurmountable one. Whether this proposed assistance to sports should come through a ministry or a department of an existing ministry is really not important. Getting something done is the big thing.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking on this particular motion moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor), I cannot help but take advantage of the opportunity to speak in a little different vein from that of most other members who have participated in the debate thus far. It has been very interesting to listen to the debate, and I have enjoyed the contributions of the various members. However, I should like to offer some remarks upon the subject from a different slant. In order to do so and to fully cover the field of sport and its importance to the survival of a nation, it is necessary to start with the early history of Rome.
In the early days of Roman history we read there was no system of public education. All instructions given to the Roman youth were given by the father to the son. This instruction consisted of training in the manly sports such as running, swimming, boxing, wrestling and the use of arms. There was also practical training in agricultural pursuits. They were taught a knowledge of the traditions of the state and the legends of Roman heroes. The son was given instructions in habits of cleanliness and good conduct. At 18 the young Roman entered military service where he was taught discipline and respect for authority, a very important thing.
The downfall of Rome started when the simple life gave way to high living and extravagance. There was vigorous opposition from the champions of the old simple life, but the Roman civilization continued to decay. The rich citizens who controlled Rome had their luxuries, and they had their summer homes just as we do today. It may be said that just as corruption characterized the public life of Rome, so did extravagance and a life of luxury characterize the well-to-do. Some 320,000 male citizens were receiving the dole, free bread, and their votes were

courted by free passes to the coliseum. In other words, in those days there was political bribery occurring.
Between 96 A.D. and 180 A.D. the Roman empire reached its peak in territorial expansion, population and material prosperity. The fall of Rome is no great mystery. Rome became a spectator nation. As we read history we find that they became fat and lazy. They depended on the dole, and in many ways the rich engaged only in spectator sports. They built large coliseums in which these sports events were presented. In 186 B.C. they had a wild beast hunt, and the first exhibition of the gladiators was given at a funeral in 264 B.C. Then, as the hunger of the Roman people for blood grew, they started pitting men against beasts in the arena, about which we all read no doubt in school.
As these types of exhibitions became popular, they exercised a brutalizing effect on the spectators. The Roman people, as we know, reached the point where they scorned the obvious lessons from the history of Greece. The Greeks, of course, were tremendous sport enthusiasts. They used sport as a means of building up their youth. As the Romans became rich and lazy, they scorned these activities and they became prey to other nations.
Now, going on a little farther in history we find that the greatest conquests of all were those of Genghis Khan. Genghis was tall, vigorous and had a strong build and constitution at the age of 56. This may interest some people. He believed in doing things in moderation. His favourite pleasures were polo and the chase. He never let drinking become a vice. He is alleged to have said that if you were unable to abstain from drinking, a man might get drunk three times a month. If he does it more than three times, he is criminal. If he gets drunk twice a month, it is better; if once a month, that is still more laudable. If one does not drink at all, what could be better. If such a man were found, he would be worthy of the highest esteem.
Today we heard one hon. member mention television and refer to the fact that his youngsters, instead of being interested in going out and engaging in sports would lie on the floor and watch television. After reading the history of the mighty Khan, I would say that he would throw every television set out of his country because he certainly would never allow anything to interfere with the health of his nation. As you know, the Mongolian nation was responsible for the greatest conquests, even greater than those of Alexander the Great. The most tremendous conquests ever known in history were made under this famous Khan.

The youngsters of this nation were taught to ride at the age of three, when their mothers tied them to the saddle. They were given a bow and arrow-probably a small one-at the age of four. They were encouraged to go hunting, as much time as possible spent on horseback; and even before then they were given regular bows and arrows and taught to shoot at targets.
It is an interesting thing to note that the bow used by a Mongol warrior required a pull of 166 pounds. That is considerably more than the English bow. Nowadays if you go to buy a bow the average pull or weight that you would ask for in a bow would be from 35 pounds to 40 pounds. Some of the stronger men use one nowadays with a pull of from 50 pounds to 60 pounds. The bows and arrows of today are effective from 25 yards to 50 yards. We have quite a difference there. Our strongest bow would be 60 yards. These Mongols pulled a bow that required 166 pounds of pull and they were destructive at a range from 200 yards to 300 yards. There is a tremendous difference. They were mighty bowmen. They lived on the range. Some of these Mongol warriors would sleep all night while their horses grazed. They were known to travel in two days 180 miles on horseback, which is a tremendous thing. These men were able to do these things because of sports.
Strange to say in those days the mighty Khan had rules of sportsmanship. There were certain rules in sportsmanship, certain things that were fair and certain ones that were not fair. It is a known fact, according to history, that some of these men who were poor sports lost their lives because of poor sportsmanship or in other words for not regarding the rules of sportsmanship. Fair play apparently was one of the big things in that day and it paid off in a considerable way.
It is said in history that while on a visit to Cathay the mighty Khan, before he sought to invest those countries, noticed the decay in the towns, noticed that people were interested in life only, in eating, drinking and enjoying themselves but not taking part in any type of sports at all. All the way through the history of that mighty conqueror we find that he was always outnumbered tremendously by the opposing army but that his strength lay in the fact that he had well-trained men of endurance, men who played games as a training.
They conquered Russia; they went into Russia. We find that Germany tried going into Russia in the winter. Back farther in history Napoleon went into Russia and tried to conquer Russia in winter time. We know

Sports-Proposed Establishment of Council what happened there. However, according to history, the Mongols went into Russia in two winter campaigns and conquered Russia. That was a tremendous thing back in those days. One of the reasons for his success was that his men were up-to-date, strong and played at sports. Not until the year 1260 did his descendants begin to forget his ideas on sport and good health. Then the great Mongolian empire started to break up. The interesting point is that the Mongols owed much of their success to social and economic decay in the countries they attacked, or in other words the countries they conquered in a good many cases were in a state of decay.
We now come back to early Britain. Sports in early Britain built up a tremendous country; there is no getting away from that fact. We have heard it said that the battle of Waterloo was won on the fields of Eaton and that could be quite true. On examining sports we find a little different picture. In England in the early days the nobility engaged in various types of sports, in their tournaments and things like that, whereas the men in the ranks used the broad sword, the long bow and the cross bow. This was not true in many of the other countries of the time. The only people in the other countries who engaged in the hunt or in sport were the noblemen. Therefore, it goes without saying that the British armies in the early days were much stronger because sports were played within their ranks. In the navy we find in the olden times that the mighty Drake with the Spanish armada approaching, continued to play a game of bowls. It did not worry him that this mighty armada was coming. They would outnumber him but it did not bother him a bit for the simple reason that he knew that all the men on his boat had been trained in competition in sports. There were prizes and special issues of rum for gun crews which could run a gun out faster than the others. The man who could climb to the top of the mast the fastest would get a certain prize. There were even prizes for dancing the hornpipe and various things. These pursuits made them a free-wheeling, easy-going bunch of men in the navy of that time who had nothing to worry about. We know that in that age Britain had the whole world against her at various times but still was able to survive.
In world war I there is an interesting thing to be noted in connection with our war aces. I refer to the first four of them. I could name them but I think everyone here knows them. When you begin to look into the lives of these men you will find that they came from Manitoba, from British Columbia, and from Ontario, and that they were all experts in

sports. They played sports. Another interesting thing I find is that many of them were great at hunting. They were very handy with a shotgun and with a rifle; they were tremendous shots. Sports gave them this tremendous advantage. Our leading ace Bishop was a tremendous shot. His great ability in the air was due to his shooting more than to his flying, although he was a very good pilot. Owing to the fact that these men had played sports, they had nothing to worry about at all.
I was in the air force in world war I and I remember that every Wednesday at four o'clock we washed out and played games. It was considered to be important that we do so. Even at that time there was a demand for men. Our country was in a rather bad spot and was needing men trained. Instead of doing that, it was considered necessary that we wash out Wednesday afternoons and play games. We played baseball, hockey and various games to build up our abilities in order to be ready for the time when we went to war.
A few months after the war was over I was offered an opportunity to go to China to teach flying. A friend of mine by the name of Brown was flying at a school in China and he wanted me to go over and teach the Chinese to fly. I asked him at the time what kind of pupils the Chinese made. He said they were tremendous, but he said that the Japanese made their wills and kissed the family good-bye before they went up as they figured that fate had decided that they were through on that particular trip.
It is quite interesting to note that on Vancouver island an attempt was made to get a Jap in a camp there to run a big caterpillar tractor. The authorities could not find any of the Japs that could run it for the simple reason that none of them had played sports at anytime. This may not sound sensible but it is a fact. They were very much afraid of this tremendous monster of a "cat" and they could not master it. Finally at Union Bay they found a Jap boy and with a little bit of training they broke the Jap in on it. Finally it was found that the boy had played baseball on the Union Bay team, that he had played basketball up there and that he had taken part in sports to such an extent that he was better able than were the others to adapt himself to running this big "cat".
Another interesting thing we remember with regard to world war II is the fact that the Japanese air force made a tremendous name for Japan. Their pilots went in, I believe, and sank some of our topnotch boats. We know what they did at Pearl Harbor. They were men to be reckoned with.

The thought in the air force at that time was that the Japanese pilot was tremendous. However, when these pilots were killed off, we found that Japan's air force was nothing from then on. What happened was that all the pilots that had gone to the University of California, the University of Washington, the University of British Columbia, the University of Alberta, the University of Toronto, who played sports had been killed off, and they got back to the pilots who had not played various types of sports. That was the end in world war II of an effective Japanese air force.
Another point I want to make with regard to this motion which the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has presented is this. The battle of Britain was another demonstration. Some of the participants have been members here. If you examined the background of a lot of these men you would find that they played sports. They were experts, and that made them second to none as pilots, and they held back the mighty German air force. I do not want to talk about war because I do not believe in wars. I have had enough, as we all have, of war, and I do not think we will be engaged in another war for years. I want to get away from that and talk a little bit about sports, and what it has to do with the people of today.
I was quite interested in a little clipping which I have here about Anne Heggtveit, the skier, who recently came back after doing such a tremendous job. Let me point out one or two things which I think are quite good. It says:
If the present situation isn't changed, she predicted "the top skiers in the world in the next six or eight years will be Russians and red Chinese, because their governments make it possible for them to ski full-time."
Anne started skiing at two and represented Canada in the world championship when only 15. That is what happened right along the line. I might say that somebody started her skiing at two. I would imagine it was her parents. It is very much like the Mongols fastening their youngsters on a horse at the age of three. I started my daughter skating at the age of three, and I believe it is a marvellous thing for her. This is a girl who has made a name for herself for the simple reason that her parents took an interest in her and felt that her health would be better if she went out and did skiing.
I also notice that these news reporters often sound a warning to us, and in saying that I mean they certainly are presenting a warning to Canada that we must make sure that people who are able to ski will get the backing.

Mr. Speaker, my first remarks, of course, must be words of congratulation to my friend, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor) who has introduced this resolution. As we are fully aware now, the hon. member has done a great deal of research into a subject which has been very close to him for many years. Despite the differences that we may have regarding details of the resolution I know that many hon. members in this house and certainly those who have spoken join with me in congratulating him on taking the lead in bringing to our attention at this time a resolution of this nature.
I debated however if I should comment about the fact of whether or not the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard should be congratulated on a recent sports event in which he was engaged for I understand that he served as captain to a rather unfortunate hockey team which was defeated-some 14 goals to 2-by the protective staff; but his inability to perform efficiently on the ice in no way detracts from his ability to offer to the Canadian people something of value in the nature of this resolution.
In discussing the proposal for the establishment of a Canada sports council I wish to make two points which I shall put in the form of questions. Should the Canada sports council be modelled on the Canada Council? What results could be obtained from this? Before amplifying these questions, I feel obliged to make some reference to the contribution to this debate made by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) who this afternoon provided to the discussion what is generally termed as comic relief. Perhaps his contribution could also be described as humour, although it was humour
[Mr. Grills.)
of a low grade. I have no objection to humour of this kind but I feel it is unfortunate that any hon. member of this house should take it upon himself to be humorous at the expense of other people. Perhaps the one regret the hon. gentleman has is that his days in this chamber are numbered and his contribution to the Canadian scene will soon be forgotten whereas Canadian people will remember the contributions made to both professional and amateur sports fields by people who were the victims of his remarks long after the hon. member has returned to the honourable profession of teaching school. I should like to say to him that if he had any understanding of the contributions made by people like Smythe and Dutton not only to sports but to society as a whole he surely would not have been so willing to stick his neck out as he did because his remarks make him look even more ridiculous than usual and he has a capacity for this.

And then he did not have the intestinal fortitude to do other than say he would abstain from voting.
I am now going on to discuss the proposed resolution in a constructive way and refer to those aspects of it which I consider of particular importance. I am certain that the hon. member who proposed the resolution will agree with me when I say that there is an area of weakness in it. He has already accepted that, and when the government eventually gives consideration to the matter from the point of view of putting something on the statute books of Canada they will have to take these shortcomings into account. The resolution is not intended as the whole answer but rather as a partial solution to a very difficult problem.
It should be emphasized that the resolution was not designed as the whole answer. It is not designed to make professional sports as such more professional. The debate so far has rather centred around the two principal sports of football and hockey. When we are talking about the varieties of athletic endeavours in which Canadians engage it must be kept in mind that we have a greater combination than any other country in the

world and there is participation by our young people on a wider basis than in any other country.
We hear a great deal, for example, about the plight, as it has been described by some of the old timers in hockey, of the young people who today play on the rinks of Canada. What we overlook is that today there are some 96,000 young Canadians registered with the Canadian amateur hockey association, 17,000 more than at any other time in our history. These young Canadians are taking advantage of the natural and artificial ice made available to them. I for one do not sit in judgment on the young people who have decided that their choice is to take part in such games. If they prefer to curl, play golf or take advantage of any other recreational pursuit of that type, that is a decision which I suggest we can leave to them.
Having said that, I should like to point out what I hope are certain advantages embodied in the resolution, but first of all perhaps I might deal with its shortcomings. This resolution has been modelled after that preceding the establishment of the Canada Council. The hon. member who introduced the resolution made it very clear that there should be the least possible amount of government control in legislation of this kind, and I agree with him. It is significant to note that 22 years ago a rather similar debate took place. At that time the then hon. member for Trinity introduced a resolution which read as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, in the interests of public health there should be established a ministry of sports.
At that time he could not obtain the support of his own colleagues, let alone other members of the house. I think I can best describe the opposition to it by quoting the words of the then minister of pensions and national health, Hon. C. G. Power, when he said, as found at page 124 of Hansard for January 20, 1937:
-I doubt very much whether any nation reared and strengthened on individual effort as Canada has been from the time of our pioneer forefathers, requires any governmental or governing body to teach the youth of this country whether they should or should not play hockey, football or lacrosse.
I believe that the then minister of pensions and national health summed up the position that some of us in the house today would
take, that we should not ask any government to interfere, to regulate or be responsible for the administration of athletic endeavour in any shape or form. The resolution before us does not call for that. It would place firmly defined responsibility in the hands of a select body to be appointed, but a body which in no way would be answerable to the decisions, whether political or otherwise, of any government administration.
The weakness of any body completely apart from government influence is the same weakness from which the Canada Council suffers today. As recently as today I read a press release advising that the Canada Council has approved a grant to an individual to attend in Pittsburgh, of all places, a workshop where he may study to be a critic. With a sports council we might run into difficulties of the same kind in making awards and giving help from the point of view of determining how policy can best assist individuals. There would be the problem of determining how much should be granted and for what objectives. Geographic considerations would enter into the making of decisions and it would have to be decided what policy we were going to have toward groups which to a very large degree are self-supporting such as semiamateurs or "shamateurs" or whatever you want to call them. That is one weakness that I see in the suggestion but I think that there is certainly an answer.
But let us go on to the advantages. How can a sports council assist? What can it accomplish? First of all, I do not believe that we should necessarily place the emphasis on sending teams to compete in international events throughout the world. I think there is a far more important objective. That sounds like a great, round platitude but let me explain it. There are in Canada today a number of organizations such as one in my own city known as the Canadian Olympic development committee. This applies equally to the sporting scene.
Fourthly, I think that this council could carry out recreational training, something which was attempted in the legislation of 1944 to which reference has already been made, an act to establish a national council of physical fitness. I think it was said by one of the hon. members who has taken part in this debate, that that legislation failed. I suppose the record will show this to be true. However, he went on to say that no effort was made to take action. A great many of the provinces, Mr. Speaker, did take advantage of that measure. Possibly if it did fail it failed largely because of the one thing which the mover of the present resolution before us said he did not want introduced into his


council, that is a large measure of government regulation. We in the province of Alberta were able to use it to a degree in cooperation with our cities in the province. We carried out a recreational program which is today being continued, largely as a result of the initiative lent by this measure.
What I say is that this sports council should be responsible at the national level for a degree of recreational training, or the supervision of it. I suggest that this could become one of its most important functions because, in fact, while the sports council would be concerned not with the professional, but to a degree with international competition, but a large measure of its responsibility will be in youth training, the development of our youngsters and making them understand the meaning of competition, the meaning of being able to grow up in a community and enjoy the facilities which I suggest this council should help to provide.
Fifth, I suggest the council could provide a very substantial amount of promotion and research. We, today, have seen many examples of particular types of athletic endeavour which could be usefully employed, not only as a means of creating a vehicle to enjoy the sport but also for creating an element of national unity, such as my own city created in 1948 in connection with the Grey cup. Unless you are going to be able to carry out promotion and research, which is so essential to all these youths, then they will flounder around on their own. There will be no planing to it. This is an area in which they could certainly receive some help.
Sixth, I suggest that this council could be of help in the promotion of any major sports undertaking. In this house we have already had references to the pan-American games, but the proposition with which I am immediately concerned is that of bringing to Canada its first major contest other than on a Commonwealth basis, the winter Olympics. This event could be staged in the area of Banff-Calgary in 1968. I might be excused if I made a reference to this particular undertaking. Perhaps I might tell the house the way in which I think the government could usefully employ whatever funds it may be able to give to such an undertaking. Perhaps I could give you some idea of the magnitude of the problem that faces a community that wishes to sponsor something of this nature.
It is perhaps well known to the house that very shortly, in 1960, the Olympic games will be going to an area which is known as Squaw Valley in the state of California in the United States. They expect something like 35,000 spectators and about 2,000 contestants. They have already embarked on capital projects

costing about $8 million. They have obtained $4 million from the state of California and $4 million from the federal treasury of the United States. Let me say very quickly that it is not the intention of the Calgary Olympic committee to come to this government for $4 million. What I can say is this: that the investment which Squaw Valley will eventually have in an area which I have heard described as perhaps one of the most unsuitable in the world for the staging of the winter Olympic games, is something that will turn it into a revenue producing centre for the entire state, in fact the entire country, for many years to come.
In the area of Banff national park and lake Louise we have already many of the essential facilities that the $8 million will have to provide in Squaw Valley. We have already many facilities which are equal to or better than Olympic standards. We have already much of the accommodation, much of the organization, and later in July of this year, with the full sanction of the Canadian Olympic association, the committee will present its bid for the 1968 winter Olympics. If this group is successful, it will make a national park of Canada the centre of skiing, not only as a sporting attraction but as a spectator attraction, on the North American continent. If they are successful, and I have every reason to believe they will be, they will turn an area which has been able to benefit from summer sporting events into a two-season area, an all year round sporting area, which will make it a very prosperous centre and the returns or dividends payable to the government will, in themselves, be worth the effort to promote the undertaking.
Here is the point I wish to make. If an undertaking of this nature is to be successful, it would perhaps best have been encouraged by the establishment of a sports council which would have been able to provide much of the research which was necessary and which we, in western Canada, provided for ourselves. It would have been able to assist more adequately in problems having to do with history of the problems of past Olympic games. It would have been able to give some consideration to whether or not many of the ideas that we have are practicable, based on experience over the years, and by having a pool of information from which we could draw. This group that is sponsoring the event will have spent about three years before they are in a position to come to ask for any federal help. It would have been of great assistance to this body to have had the co-operation and assistance for which the province and federal government eventually will be asked. This is
the only area in Canada that is in a position to stage an attraction of this type.
I do not intend to labour this point any further. After the selection has been made you will, in due course, hear a complete report from the international Olympic committee. They will reveal the complete plans for the staging, as I said at the outset, of the first international major attraction in Canada in our entire history.
I shall now make one or two references to the situation on the sporting scene with respect to our athletes and our major sports attractions today. I suggest that this is one reason for the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard introducing this resolution. I think he was concerned, if I may say so, with the growing area in which our athletes were not able to compete on an equal basis because they were ill-trained. He was concerned about the way in which we were beginning to lose our desire as a nation to compete. It is a natural desire to want to take some action. I suggest to him that the Canada sports council is indeed a move in the right direction, but it is only one of the moves that should be made. Part of the responsibility must also rest on those people who are today organizing the sporting scene in Canada.
I suggest that part of the responsibility- and a large part of it-must rest with those who insist on overlapping one sporting attraction with another so that in many Canadian cities today you can see a hockey game, a football game and a baseball game all in the same week. I suggest there is a responsibility on those who organize the sporting scene in our cities, a responsibility to get together to eliminate, wherever possible, the seventy-game hockey schedule which runs into May and which competes with baseball and so cannot survive, and baseball cannot survive eventually with a competing football season.
Surely this is not just a government responsibility. The responsibility must rest on those who are promoting the various athletic programs which we enjoy. I also suggest that there is a responsibility falling on those groups who are to some degree pricing themselves out by the sporting field. There are so many dollars available for those who wish to take in any number of attractions. We have found that many of our young men and young women-and this is so not only in connection with professional sports but in connection with many of our amateur programs-are not able to provide the necessary funds with which to enjoy the broad variety which is available to them today.
I suggest that our provincial governments have a responsibility with respect to endeavouring to encourage many of our amateur

I suggest that our sporting organizations should endeavour to get together to restore some of the major contests such as the Allan Cup games to the place they occupied in the Canadian sporting scene just a few years ago. Today the young man or the young boy who is competing in any number of events looks at what eventually will be his maximum reward which is not measured in dollars and cents but in recognition. The day that the Allan Cup was literally destroyed, amateur hockey nearly died with it.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian public, those who pay their way to see the show, and those who are responsible for the organization of our major sporting enterprises, those attractions which we see from time to time, also have a responsibility and one in which they must also give some leadership before the government can be expected to undertake something of this size.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, let me close perhaps on this note. The mover of this resolution gave us what I thought was a broad and comprehensive picture of the need. He presented enough evidence to show that there was a demand to do something. Perhaps it may be said that the timing of this resolution was not good and I think that is true. It must be placed in perspective with all the other things this government will have to do in this session of this parliament. Therefore it must be recognized that there are other priorities well ahead of this one that must be attended to. This proposal has just been suggested to the government, recognizing that it has some shortcomings in how it can be administered. However, it has been suggested that some action on a broad front be taken, not purely to produce a great many muscle bound competitors or to wave flags in international areas of sporting events but rather to provide the facilities, the training, the hope to our youth to be able to compete, and the opportunity for Canadians to avoid becoming purely a nation of spectators. As I say, this is the one hope that those who enjoy sporting events in any area have. It is the one hope they have to see that they can have something on an organized national basis.
There will be critics who will say that this is a luxury that we as Canadians cannot afford. Let me say to them that if they have any doubt about the interest there is in this matter, let them endeavour to attend any number of attractions put on by kids


in pee-wee hockey, by amateur hockey associations or other sports associations not too well known to us. Let us remember that this is a subject that commands a great deal of national attention. It is not something so local that it has no interest or no priority whatsoever. I subscribe to the view that this is a resolution which, like the whole fibre of our Canadian way of life, is made up of little things, of a culture of one type or another, a fast moving business economy, with great natural resources. I would suggest that this is just as much a part and parcel of the Canadian way of life as is anything else that we do. I suggest that it has a real place in our Canadian way of life and is something to which we can without any reservation give complete support.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this resolution this evening, I think congratulations to the member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor), who placed this motion on the order paper and who made the recommendations he made this afternoon, are certainly in order. At the outset, I would like to say that I speak in support of the motion, and I am also very happy to see today the C.C.F. party are supporting the Progressive Conservative suggestions. Before setting out a few of my comments and placing them on record, I think at this stage, as we have heard reference to this resolution, I should re-read the resolution:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give early consideration to the advisability of establishing a Canada sports council with the object of fostering and encouraging amateur sport in Canada, such council to have representatives from each of the provinces of Canada.
It need not be repeated that organized amateur sport for our young boys and girls in this country assures us that our best asset, namely our youth, will, by participation in proper amateur sport, have healthy bodies and minds and thereby become outstanding citizens. In the early Greek civilization, which I believe was referred to by one of the British Columbia members, much emphasis was put on physical training so that the citizens of the community would become leaders and take their part in the community. No one denies that sport creates leaders of character. There is, I would suggest, with our youth today a crying need for such type of council.
I wish to refer to a few things which are very personal to me because of my own profession. There is one thing with which I always agree when reference to it is made by a member of the C.C.F. party, the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) and that concerns the conditions of the jails. The reason I wish to make a few remarks on that is that I believe that amateur sport, properly
1066	HOUSE OF
Sports-Proposed Establishment of Council organized, in which the youth of this country will be able to participate, would be the greatest defence against our problem of juvenile delinquency. I think I have found that one of the most depressing things in my career as a young lawyer was to see young men and boys held in custody in some of our city and provincial jails awaiting trial, sometimes without bail. Organized amateur sport in this country, in my opinion, would be, as I said before, the greatest weapon against juvenile delinquency. We need organized sport to keep our boys, in plain language, out of trouble. These boys who are placed in custody in city and provincial jails awaiting trial because of such crimes as car theft, breaking and entering organized by youth mobs, have never really known the thrill of catching a baseball, or known the thrill of receiving the pass of a hockey puck from another teammate and scoring a goal. They have never really known the thrill of receiving a pass in a rugby game. This type of organized sport would have saved many of them from the horrible experience of being detained- and I say this without any hesitation-in outdated, drab, overcrowded, and in many cases dirty jails while they await trial, many of them without bail.
In referring to this question, I am sure John Howard of the 18th century would be shocked to see the conditions in which our youth are detained because they have been involved in something which is contrary to the law. I see many of these young men under these circumstances. In many cases their fathers and mothers ask the same question we would ask namely, "What have I done?" or "What have I left undone?" When I hear that remark I often think of the poet Matthew Arnold who dedicated the poem "Rugby Chapel" in honor of his father. His father, as you all well know, invented and created the sport known as rugby, where you receive the hard knocks, but you learn as a young man to take those knocks. That is the purpose of the game. You will recall the words he used when referring to his own father, which words I say are applicable to young men who have had the opportunity to participate in sport in our land. He said about his father-and I am sure he meant these words with reference to other men who had similar qualifications as his father-these words:
Not like the men of the crowa,
Who all round me today Bluster or cringe, and make life Hideous, and arid, and vile;
But souls tempered with fire,
Fervent, heroic and good,
Helpers and friends of mankind.


I have seen the minds of these young men who have run afoul of the law become warped, and they have become antisocial. They are against everybody and everything: they are against the world. One remembers the expression, "But for the grace of God there goes I", or "But for the grace of God there goes anyone." The type of character that Matthew Arnold described in his dedicated poem is the type of mature character which typifies the average Canadian boy which has had the opportunity of taking part in amateur sport. Boys who have participated in amateur sport are able to make good citizens, able in public relations.
There are many examples in the House of Commons of men who have taken part in amateur sport in their earlier years, and who have the same respect for the rules of debate as they have for the rules of the game in which they participated. I believe a good example of this, and I think the whole house will agree with me, is the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). No matter how hot the debate becomes, he never usurps the rules of debate, because he learnt those rules as a sportsman in his youth. I think another good example is our own Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), who is a good sportsman today and also follows in the footsteps of the Leader of the Opposition in that respect.
All of this is ample proof that there is a need for a Canadian sports council which would help organize sport throughout Canada so that every boy and girl in all walks of life would have the opportunity to take part in these games which are so important to character building. In this way we would make certain that the dollar mark would not keep a boy from participating in sports and if such boy has normal aptitude he would have the opportunity to participate in these sports, and if he had an aptitude above normal he would have the chance to excel in these sports. The dollar sign would not stand in his way irrespective of the side of the track he came from.
Such a council of Canada, fostering and encouraging amateur sport in Canada, not regulating it as was suggested by one hon. member, would be the biggest defence against juvenile delinquency. This is an asset which is wasted everytime one of our Canadian boys is incarcerated in an institution. Many of our young men and young boys who are now in custody in provincial and federal institutions would be living normal lives in society if they had had the opportunity to participate in amateur sport. They would have learned earlier the lessons which

are necessary to take their places in society and adjust to the strains of society.
I regret that there has been a tendency to let professional management coaches take the responsibility for training our young men to play hockey, football, basketball and other types of sport. I do not want to leave the impression that there is no place in society for professionals. That is the impression that I believe was left by one of the members of the C.C.F. party who spoke this afternoon. However, professional athletes are proficient performers as distinct from sportsmen as we formerly understood the term. Recently I read an article by Haig-Brown describing his experiences as a magistrate at Campbell River, British Columbia, and he had this to say, differentiating between amateur and professional sport:
A professional doesn't play a game for fun. He works at it for a living. He may be a lighthearted individual who likes to enjoy himself. He may be an honourable man who wants to observe every rule faithfully and show the utmost generosity to his opponents but he had better not let these considerations interfere too much with the business of winning or he won't be earning a living very long. He is controlled by promoters and coaches, by the press and by the paying public. If his mental attitude remains that of an amateur he cannot possibly survive his first season.
This of course may be carried further to the conclusion that only the best can take part in sports today. But I do suggest that that is the way to differentiate between the two-that today there has been a tendency to sponsor professional sport and let amateur sport go by, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith). The problem is that only the cream off the top, only the proficient performers, get that opportunity and I do think the recommendation made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard as to establishing a council to encourage and foster amateur sports so that all boys and girls in this country can have an opportunity to participate in that sport so that they can take their places in society and become leaders in some form or another is a good one.
What is needed is an organization to help the boys play hockey on the ponds and on the outdoor rinks, on the vacant lot or in the parks rather than have them governed by professional rules and regulations and have them sign contracts before they reach a mature age. Such boys serve the sport rather than the sport serving the boys. The fostering and encouraging of amateur sport in Canada will give a universal atmosphere to the whole tone of our sports program. Suggestions have also been made in this article by Haig-Brown in MacLeans magazine of May 12, 1956, in which he said:

Athletic sports are said to be character forming. They undoubtedly are-to those who play, those who watch and those who merely read about them. But they can develop shabby and dirty characteristics just as readily as they can develop sound and good ones. Some argue that the boys have changed, but I am not one who argues that the boys and girls of this generation are, basically, any different from the boys and girls of past generations. Recreational facilities in the cities are soon wiped out, youth runs afoul of the law and then has to suffer the consequences of the conditions I described at the beginning of my address. What we need, I suggest, is good honest sport organized and taught by ordinary fellows who know the game and who will give the boys plenty of space where expensive equipment is not a problem, a place where everyone can take part, an atmosphere where winning is not all important, a condition where the individual is all important and team spirit is all important; a place where the old Greek rule of thumb is the rule rather than the exception, to use no fraud and no guile in contest.
Turning just for a moment to give this a personal touch, I was happy to hear the hon. member for Calgary South-maybe this is Calgary night because the hon. member for Calgary South spoke and I see the M.L.A. from Calgary in the gallery-but I am very happy on behalf of the Bow River constituency and particularly that part around lake Louise-and I may suggest to you, those who have visited it, that it is the most beautiful playground in the world-to see that there is a movement afoot, and hope that they will ask for the world Olympics in 1968 or sooner because Banff is one of the places where such songs really make sense-where the deer and the antelope roam and where the moose roam and where the bears roam -one of the last of those places set apart in our country as a natural park where nature remains as she was from the very first times. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be very glad to forego the pleasure of speaking on this motion if I thought that by refraining I would be making a vote on it possible but I understand-and I do not complain about it

that there are a great many hon. members who wish to express their views. It is possible therefore, to say the least, doubtful whether a vote will be taken tonight. Perhaps I might be forgiven then for taking advantage of this opportunity of saying a few words about a resolution in which I confess I am very interested indeed and which I wholeheartedly support. I hope no one is going to say that I did not support it at any time during the last 10 years. I did, but not in the House of Commons.
In any event this motion merely asks the government to give early consideration to the possibility of establishing a Canada sports council. The aim of this resolution in my opinion is one which should commend itself to every hon. member of this house as I believe it does. It certainly deals with a matter in which I have been interested as long as I have been able to remember anything.

As the hon. member who has just taken his seat said, some of us in this house in days gone by have known the thrill of receiving a pass and the desolation of missing the ensuing shot or occasionally the thrill of putting it in the upper left-hand corner.
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor) for putting this resolution on the order paper and for the way he introduced it to the house this afternoon. He reminded us that we now have in this country a Canada Council and that the time has come for a Canada sports council. Indeed, he said this afternoon, and I believe I am quoting him correctly, that perhaps there was a greater need for a Canada sports council. I would not like to go so far as that myself because I can think of no greater need in Canada at the present time than government assistance to education through scholarships and through the construction of university buildings and government assistance to the cultural development of our country. Nothing, I think, can be more important than that.
But so, also, are physical fitness and a healthy interest by this country's youth in amateur sport important. Surely, it is the course of wisdom to pursue the paths of national development in both fields, the field of athletic activity and the field of cultural activity. As a matter of fact, I have heard some people rather disparage the assistance that has been given to cultural activities in this country through the Canada Council by calling it "aid to ballet dancers" but it is unnecessary to remind the house that a country, the government and the system of society in which perhaps places greater emphasis on the material development of its members than any other society-I am talking about the communist state in Russia-[DOT] places almost as great an emphasis and gives as great assistance to ballet dancing as to sport. So it is possible and it should be desirable, I suggest, to combine any government assistance to these two activities in the material and the non-material development of our country.
I would hope that when the time comes- and I think it will come-for the establishment of a council devoted to the objective of this resolution, that council in its activities and in the assistance it may get from the federal government and perhaps from provincial governments as well, will be more concerned with encouraging the youth of this country to participate-and this has been mentioned, I know, by more than one speaker today-in sports and less interested in watching sports via television.
The hon. member who moved the motion this afternoon said that one function of such

a council would be to survey the needs in this field. I believe the time has come when that should be done in one way or another. He also said another function would be for the government to supply funds and other forms of assistance, some of which he mentioned. I should like to make it clear that in this context I associate the provincial governments with anything the senior government may be able to do in this field in the future.
He also mentioned the desirability of setting up a school for coaches and he added- and I think this is of interest and importance -that a council of this kind if it should be set up could play a most useful and important part in preparing the way for our centenary celebration in 1967 by laying the groundwork for the international athletic side connected with that celebration. Perhaps to be effective it is not too soon for the government to do that now. I know the hon. member struck a responsive chord in our hearts when he mentioned that perhaps steps could be taken even now to prepare the way for Olympic, or Pan-American or British commonwealth games in Canada during that celebration.
I would hope that a council of this kind would have as its first function the encouragement and support of the participation of the youth of our country in amateur sports and to do what can be done and what certainly needs to be done to persuade them that there is more to sport than watching it through television. I would also hope that this council, if and when it is set up, could support, improve and help to organize Canada's participation in international sport. There is no doubt, and it has been mentioned by more than one speaker, that our country has slipped in recent years in this branch of international activity. I am old enough to remember the great days of Canada's participation in Olympic and international sport, especially in track and field. I think they were probably greater days than any we have known since. I remember the great days of Sherring, who won the first marathon, and Bob Kerr, both of them from Hamilton, Ed Archibald, Jack Tait and the immortal Tom Longboat. Perhaps we reached the height of our international achievement in this field of sport at the Antwerp Olympics when, as I think the hon. member who began this debate pointed out, a Vancouver sprinter won the 100 yards, won the 220 yards and a Winnipeg quarter-miler would have won the quarter mile if he had not turned around in the last ten yards to see how far the American was behind him. Since that time there is no doubt that we have not been as successful in Olympic sports as we were in those earlier days.

Even in hockey there has been a big change from the time a few Canadian students at Oxford could arm themselves with some sticks and secondhand skates, go off to the European continent and become European champions even if they had to learn to skate in Switzerland to do it. We have not been surpassed in this particular sport but other countries are catching up to us although perhaps in compensation we have made international progress in other forms of athletic activity such as swimming, golf and skiing.
You may argue that it is no part of government and it is not even a legitimate government interest to worry about international sport, but unfortunately-perhaps it is unfortunate; whether or not it is, it is true- international sport is now associated with international prestige. If it was before world war II, if it was before the 30's, it is much more now because of the determination of the totalitarian states to use achievement on the sporting field as an indication of national prowess and prestige. Therefore, although I do not suggest it should be carried too far, I think it is now a legitimate interest of government to do what it can to see that the reputation of our country is maintained on the international athletic field.
I know some of the difficulties in this regard because in our country as in some other countries we do attempt to observe the amateur rules that have been laid down for international competition and which, of course, do not mean anything in totalitarian states. I have come to the conclusion myself -I do not know whether it is a valid or right one-that the time has come when, if international sport is to be such a matter of international prestige, there should be no distinction between an amateur and a professional in representing his country in international competition. There is no such distinction in cricket which in some respects is supposed to be the most amateur of all sports so I should like to see the day when a person who represents Canada can do so irrespective of whether he is a professional or an amateur.
It is also true, and it has a bearing on the prestige aspect of international sport, that those who do represent our country in this field of activity can do a great deal of good for the prestige of Canada or they can do an equal amount of harm. Perhaps I may be permitted to say that I have had some experience in this field. I once had the privilege of taking part in international sport but I have also had the privilege of representing Canada abroad diplomatically in countries when Canadian teams would turn up. It was just as important for the prestige and the
1070	HOUSE OF
Sports[DOT]-Proposed Establishment of Council good name of Canada in respect of those competitions that our men made as good a name off the ice or off the field as they did on the ice or on the field.
The word "ambassadors" has been used a great deal in connection with this subject, and it is quite literally true. They are indeed ambassadors of Canada when they represent Canada, especially in the sport which we consider we have made peculiarly our own. They represent Canada not only on the ice but off the ice. Perhaps here is one thing that a sports council could do. When we send teams abroad to take part in international competition under international rules perhaps we should be more careful to brief them more carefully so that they know the difference between the kind of rules under which they play hockey abroad and the rules under which they play hockey in Canada for there is a very great difference between the two games. I am not criticizing the players but sometimes the inability to appreciate that difference can cause some embarrassment.
There would, of course, be difficulties in carrying out a resolution of this kind to encourage amateur sport. One of the difficulties is drawing a line and making a distinction, and it is not as easy as it used to be, between amateur and professional sport. What is an amateur these days in some sports? I have heard it said that there are some amateurs who just cannot afford to turn professional. It is true that in some sports it would be a problem for a sports council to draw the line in a way which would be satisfactory to everybody.
Perhaps hockey is the best example of that difficulty. I think one of the speakers this afternoon made some mention of this. Certainly there is a problem involved in the pressures that professionalism puts on those taking part in amateur sport at a very young age. I do not want to exaggerate but you see a boy skating on the street these days and shooting a puck against a wall. You think that he is doing it very efficiently and showing signs of coming greatness, but when you talk to him you probably find that he is on the negotiation list of the Chicago Black Hawks. While this would be a difficulty for a sports council, especially in the kind of assistance it would be asked to give, it also might provide an opportunity to bring about a better relationship in this country between professional and amateur sports.
One of the things, of course, that a council of this kind would have to do would be to provide funds, just as the Canada Council does in another field where I am sure it finds lots of difficulty, and to allocate those


funds to suitable activities. While I agree with one of the speakers I listened to this afternoon who said we should be exceedingly careful to keep government out of sport, nevertheless if government in some form or other provided funds it might be a temptation to influence the activities which were being assisted. I hope it would not be but it might be that he who pays the player will call the tune. Any sports council would have to be very careful to avoid that. It can be done and I think it is being done in the case of the Canada Council because when that council was set up, as hon. members know, the government was kept out of any direct participation in its activities. Perhaps that could be done also in the case of a sports council. I suggest that it certainly should be done that way.
The objective of the resolution would be a very desirable one if it could be achieved. It would help in the creation of physical fitness in this country. It would help to encourage the youth of the country to take part rather than watch amateur sport. It would foster that individual desire for achievement which is the basis of good sport. But I do believe that in itself the council would not do these things. It could merely assist them.
Perhaps an indication of the limitations of a council of this kind could be found in the experience of Australia. I think it will be generally accepted by those who are interested in these things that the Australians provide the most magnificent example of achievement in sport of any country in the world today. There are only about 10 million people in Australia and we know how they excel in a variety of sports. They have done this, not through assistance from government, but because they have the desire for achievement. They have the determination to get out and learn how to play games. They are encouraged mostly by voluntary organizations in connection with the games they play. I believe there is a far greater interest in Australia, not only in participation in athletics but in voluntary assistance to encourage that participation than there is in this country.
They have not got a sports council, I am informed, in Australia. They have a federal government physical fitness council which makes grants to the states and which does encourage sporting educational activities. It makes grants to international sports teams. I believe they do not have a sports council of the type which is visualized here, and yet these 10 million people in Australia have accomplished things in this field of activity which are greater than any country their size in the world. While a council of this

kind could be most helpful, it could only assist in developing participation; the skill and achievement in which must exist in the youth of the country in the first place. But this, in itself, is surely something that is worth doing.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, for these and for other reasons which I could elaborate if there were time, I should like to express my hearty support for the resolution and congratulate the member who has initiated it. I express the hope that if we are not allowed to vote on it tonight, perhaps the feeling that has been expressed in this house will make an impression upon the government and before long we will have our Canada sports council. I know, perhaps as well as most members, the demands that are made on governments these days for assistance for everything under the sun. There have to be priorities, and perhaps this may not have top priority, but I hope that when some of these other demands may be less pressing than they are at the present time the government, with the feeling of the house as expressed this afternoon and evening in this debate before it, will be able to take up this matter. Then, perhaps we may have the pleasure of welcoming in this house the establishment of a sports council for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that we have had the pleasure of listening to a great number of speakers who have debated this resolution in its various aspects. Some have placed the emphasis upon juvenile delinquency, others on professional sports, others on group sports and still others on sports involving individual participation. In looking at this resolution it is my opinion that the only way in which it can be considered in all its aspects is from the viewpoint of the welfare of the people. What does this resolution attempt to do in so far as the people themselves are concerned? In what way does it affect their welfare?
If one considers the resolution in this light, it actually breaks down into three distinct aspects. There is one part that deals with recreation, that is those sports which may be called non-action sports; the second one deals with physical fitness; and the third aspect of this resolution deals with sports in general or what might be termed action sports.
In considering the first aspect which this resolution covers, and which I feel is the field of recreation, it is recognized I believe by everyone that at the present time there is a lack of facilities for the provision of recreation, especially for our senior citizens
Sports-Proposed Establishment of Council and those who are disabled or unable to actively participate in sports. This problem of the lack of recreational facilities, of course, is within provincial jurisdiction. Although such a council as is envisaged by this resolution, which would be set up in conjunction with the provinces, could deal with this field of recreation, I submit that the problem here is solely the lack of adequate finances. The problem in this field could be solved simply by the government, if it wished, making a grant to the provinces which would enable them to supply these additional recreational facilities. I believe that that is the problem, in essence, with regard to recreation.
Turning now to the field of physical fitness, which this resolution covers and which is a very important matter in Canada today, I think many members of this house will recall the National Physical Fitness Act, which was in force in this country for a good many years, but which was repealed in June, 1954. This act, I am sure, was set up with the good intention of promoting and increasing national interest in physical fitness. Although some useful work was performed under this act in co-ordinating physical fitness programs in the provinces, it is readily apparent that the program itself was a failure. The division set up under this act was originally set up to work on physical education, but ever so gradually it drifted into adult education, drama and other cultural fields. However, even if we say that this act was a failure in itself, that does not mean that there is no need in Canada today for some active steps to alleviate the present condition in connection with physical fitness across this country.
I am sure many hon. members of this house are not aware that our own department of health and welfare is actively concerned with this problem of physical fitness. At the present time, they have developed the Canadian physical efficiency tests in order to provide a practical means whereby individual basic physical efficiency may be assessed with due regard to age, sex and physique. These tests at the present time, or so I am told, are being conducted in many provinces. I know the department hopes that this testing project will be completed and standards developed during the present year. Our own department of health and welfare is aware of this problem and is attempting at this time to set up some sort of basis upon which a comparison may be made in order to ascertain where we stand in relation to other countries. When these tests have been completed the information then available to us will give us a better indication of the state of our physical fitness on a national scale.
